◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A random variable assigns a number to each outcome of a random experiment. Expected value (E[X]) and variance (Var(X)) are how we summarize a random variable's behavior — center and spread of the distribution. Every probability distribution and every Monte Carlo simulation reduces to computing or estimating these. The DataCamp exam tests E[X] / Var(X) calculations, linearity of expectation, and transformations.

What a random variable is

RANDOM VARIABLE (RV)
A function that assigns a number to each outcome of a random experiment.

Discrete: takes on countable values (0, 1, 2, ...)
Examples: number of heads in 10 flips; customer count today; dice roll.

Continuous: takes on any value in an interval
Examples: height; response time; temperature. 
# Roll a die — X = the value shown
# X is a discrete RV with possible values {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}

# Each value has a probability — the PMF (probability mass function)
# P(X=1) = 1/6
# P(X=2) = 1/6
# ...
# P(X=6) = 1/6

# Flip 3 coins — X = number of heads
# X possible values: {0, 1, 2, 3}
# P(X=0) = 1/8 (TTT)
# P(X=1) = 3/8 (HTT, THT, TTH)
# P(X=2) = 3/8 (HHT, HTH, THH)
# P(X=3) = 1/8 (HHH)
# Note: probabilities sum to 1

Expected value — the mean of a random variable

EXPECTED VALUE (DISCRETE)

E[X] = Σ xᵢ × P(X = xᵢ)

A weighted average: each possible value times its probability, summed.

Continuous: replace the sum with an integral over the PDF.
E[X] is also called μ (the population mean). 
# Die roll
# E[X] = 1*(1/6) + 2*(1/6) + 3*(1/6) + 4*(1/6) + 5*(1/6) + 6*(1/6)
# = (1+2+3+4+5+6) / 6
# = 21/6 = 3.5
# The "expected" value is 3.5 — even though you can never roll a 3.5
# E[X] is the LONG-RUN AVERAGE over many trials

# 3-coin flips, X = number of heads
# E[X] = 0*(1/8) + 1*(3/8) + 2*(3/8) + 3*(1/8)
# = 0 + 3/8 + 6/8 + 3/8 = 12/8 = 1.5
# Average heads per 3-flip trial = 1.5

# Lottery ticket — $1 cost, P(win)=1/1000, jackpot=$500
# E[net profit] = (500-1)*(1/1000) + (-1)*(999/1000)
# = 0.499 - 0.999
# = -$0.50
# Expected to lose 50 cents per ticket — average over many plays

Expected value of a function of X

# E[g(X)] = Σ g(xᵢ) × P(X = xᵢ)
# Apply the function to each value, then weight by probability

# Example: E[X²] for the die
# = 1²*(1/6) + 2²*(1/6) + ... + 6²*(1/6)
# = (1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + 25 + 36) / 6
# = 91/6 ≈ 15.17

# IMPORTANT: E[X²] ≠ (E[X])²
# Here: E[X²] = 15.17 but (E[X])² = 3.5² = 12.25
# This difference IS the variance (next section)

Linearity of expectation

LINEARITY OF EXPECTATION
For any random variables X, Y and constants a, b:

E[aX + b] = a × E[X] + b

E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y]

Holds even if X and Y are NOT independent. This is why it's so powerful. 
# Roll two dice; X = first roll, Y = second roll
# E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] = 3.5 + 3.5 = 7
# (Whether or not the rolls are independent — they happen to be)

# Tax on income: T = 0.25 * Income - 1000
# E[T] = 0.25 * E[Income] - 1000

# Sum of 10 coin flips (X = number of heads)
# X = X1 + X2 + ... + X10 where each Xi is 0 or 1
# E[Xi] = 0.5 (probability of heads)
# E[X] = 10 × 0.5 = 5
# Even though direct calculation requires the binomial PMF, linearity solves it instantly.

# Useful trick for harder problems:
# Decompose into indicators, take expectations, sum

Variance of a random variable

VARIANCE FORMULAS

Var(X) = E[(X − μ)²]

Computational shortcut:

Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])²

Always non-negative. Zero only if X is constant (no randomness).
Same units as X² — square root gives the standard deviation σ. 
# Die roll
# E[X] = 3.5
# E[X²] = 91/6 (from above)
# Var(X) = E[X²] - (E[X])² = 91/6 - (3.5)² = 91/6 - 12.25
# = 15.167 - 12.25 = 2.917

# Standard deviation = sqrt(2.917) ≈ 1.708

# 3-coin flips, X = number of heads
# E[X] = 1.5
# E[X²] = 0²*(1/8) + 1²*(3/8) + 2²*(3/8) + 3²*(1/8)
# = 0 + 3/8 + 12/8 + 9/8 = 24/8 = 3
# Var(X) = 3 - (1.5)² = 3 - 2.25 = 0.75
# SD(X) = sqrt(0.75) ≈ 0.866

Variance under linear transformation

VARIANCE OF aX + b

Var(aX + b) = a² × Var(X)

Multiplying by a scales variance by a² (or SD by |a|).
Adding a constant b doesn't change variance — it just shifts everything. 
# Convert die to "double or nothing": Y = 2X
# Var(Y) = 2² × Var(X) = 4 × 2.917 ≈ 11.67
# SD(Y) = 2 × SD(X) ≈ 3.42

# Add a flat bonus to every salary: New = Salary + 5000
# Var(New) = Var(Salary) — bonus doesn't change variability

# Convert Fahrenheit to Celsius: C = (5/9)(F - 32)
# Var(C) = (5/9)² × Var(F)
# SD(C) = (5/9) × SD(F)

Variance of a SUM — depends on independence

VARIANCE OF X + Y

Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2 × Cov(X, Y)

If independent, covariance is zero:

Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y)

Variance of a DIFFERENCE has the same formula:

Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) − 2 × Cov(X, Y)

Note the SUM of variances even for differences — variances don't subtract. 
# Two independent dice
# Var(X1 + X2) = Var(X1) + Var(X2) = 2.917 + 2.917 = 5.833
# SD(X1 + X2) ≈ 2.415

# Sum of n iid coin flips, Xi ∈ {0, 1} with p=0.5
# Var(Xi) = 0.25
# Var(X1 + ... + Xn) = n × 0.25
# E.g., n=100: variance = 25, SD = 5

# Compare to n × Xi (multiplying one flip by n)
# Var(n*X1) = n² × 0.25 = 25 (for n=100, = 2500)
# SD = 50

# So: SUMMING n independent copies has variance n × Var(one)
# MULTIPLYING by n has variance n² × Var(one)
# Random fluctuations of summed independent samples grow with √n, NOT n
# This is why averages get more precise as n grows: SD of mean = SD / √n

Worked example — expected profit and risk

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Investment decision

Scenario: An investment has three possible outcomes:

  • P(big win) = 0.10 → return $10,000
  • P(small win) = 0.40 → return $1,000
  • P(loss) = 0.50 → return −$500

Should you invest? Compute E[X] and Var(X).

import numpy as np

returns = np.array([10000, 1000, -500])
probs = np.array([0.10, 0.40, 0.50])

# Expected value
E_X = np.sum(returns * probs)
# = 1000 + 400 - 250 = 1150

# E[X²]
E_X2 = np.sum(returns**2 * probs)
# = 10_000_000 + 400_000 + 125_000 = 10_525_000

# Variance and SD
var_X = E_X2 - E_X**2 # 10_525_000 - 1_322_500 = 9_202_500
sd_X = np.sqrt(var_X) # ≈ 3034

# Decision context:
# Expected profit: $1,150 per investment
# Standard deviation: $3,034 — large compared to expectation
# Coefficient of variation: 3034 / 1150 ≈ 2.6 — very high

# Conclusion: positive expected return BUT the variability is huge
# A single investment is risky; many independent investments would average out

Covariance and correlation

COVARIANCE

Cov(X, Y) = E[(X − μ_X)(Y − μ_Y)] = E[XY] − E[X] × E[Y]

Positive: when X above its mean, Y tends to be above too.
Negative: when X above mean, Y tends to be below.
Zero: no linear relationship.

Correlation (next chapter) = covariance scaled to be unitless: ρ = Cov(X,Y) / (σ_X × σ_Y), range −1 to 1. 
import numpy as np

# Simulate two correlated variables
n = 10000
x = np.random.normal(0, 1, n)
y = 0.7 * x + 0.5 * np.random.normal(0, 1, n) # y depends on x plus noise

cov = np.cov(x, y, ddof=1)[0, 1] # ~0.7
corr = np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1] # ~0.8 (unitless)

# Or in pandas
df.cov() # covariance matrix
df.corr() # correlation matrix

Estimating E[X] and Var(X) from data

import numpy as np

# Sample from a population — use sample statistics to estimate population parameters
sample = np.array([2, 5, 7, 8, 4, 6, 9, 3, 5, 6])

# Sample mean estimates E[X]
x_bar = sample.mean() # = 5.5

# Sample variance (ddof=1) estimates Var(X)
sample.var(ddof=1) # = 4.94
# Or: np.var(sample, ddof=1)

# Sample SD
sample.std(ddof=1) # ≈ 2.22

# As n grows, sample stats converge to true E[X] and Var(X) — law of large numbers
# For Monte Carlo: run many simulations, take the mean
n_trials = 100_000
results = np.random.normal(loc=10, scale=2, size=n_trials) # simulated experiment
results.mean() # estimate of E[X]
results.var(ddof=1) # estimate of Var(X)

Common expectation/variance mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Confusing E[X²] with (E[X])² — the gap between them IS the variance
  2. Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) when not independent — must add 2*Cov(X,Y)
  3. Var(X − Y) = Var(X) − Var(Y) — WRONG; subtraction adds variances for independent X, Y
  4. Forgetting Var(aX) = a² × Var(X) — the square matters
  5. Assuming linearity for nonlinear functions — E[X²] ≠ (E[X])², E[1/X] ≠ 1/E[X]
  6. Sample variance: forgetting ddof=1 — NumPy default is 0; pandas default is 1
  7. Treating expected value as a "likely outcome" — E[X] = 3.5 for a die isn't possible to roll
  8. Confusing the variance of a single RV with variance of the mean — Var(X̄) = Var(X) / n
★ ON THE EXAM

"E[X] formula?" → Sum of value × probability for discrete RVs.

"E[aX + b]?" → a × E[X] + b. Always.

"E[X + Y]?" → E[X] + E[Y]. Holds even when NOT independent.

"Var(X) formula?" → E[X²] − (E[X])², or E[(X − μ)²].

"Var(aX + b)?" → a² × Var(X). The b doesn't matter.

"Var(X + Y) for independent X, Y?" → Var(X) + Var(Y).

"Var(X − Y) for independent X, Y?" → Var(X) + Var(Y) — still ADD.

"E[X²] = (E[X])²?" → Only if Var(X) = 0 (X is constant).

"E[X] = sample mean as n → ∞?" → Yes (law of large numbers).

"SD of the mean?" → SD(X) / √n — decreases with √n.

"Cov = 0?" → Linearly uncorrelated; doesn't necessarily mean independent.

"Bernoulli(p): E[X] and Var(X)?" → p and p(1−p).

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Random variable: a function mapping outcomes to numbers; can be discrete or continuous
  • Expected value E[X] is the probability-weighted average — the long-run mean
  • E[X] = Σ x × P(X = x) for discrete RVs
  • Linearity: E[aX + b] = a × E[X] + b; E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] — works even without independence
  • Variance Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])² — gap between mean of squares and square of mean
  • Var(aX + b) = a² × Var(X); the b cancels out
  • Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2 × Cov(X, Y); for independent X, Y the covariance term is zero
  • Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) − 2 × Cov(X, Y); variances ADD even for subtractions of independents
  • Standard deviation σ = √Var(X) — same units as X
  • Standard deviation of the sample mean: σ / √n (gets tighter with more data)
  • Sample variance with ddof=1 is unbiased estimator of population variance
  • Common distributions have memorized E and Var formulas (Bernoulli p, p(1−p); Binomial np, np(1−p); etc.)
  • Covariance measures linear relationship; correlation = covariance scaled to [−1, 1]

Linearity of expectation: E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] — ALWAYS, even when X and Y are dependent. No independence needed — the expectation of a sum equals the sum of expectations, full stop.

📊 FIGURE — Expected value is the balance point
Put equal 1/6 weights at 1 through 6 and the beam balances at 3.5 — the expected value Σx·P(x). E[X] need not be a possible outcome (you never roll 3.5); it is the long-run average of many rolls.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Real data falls into recognizable patterns. Successes/failures = Bernoulli/Binomial. Rare-event counts = Poisson. Time-to-first-success = Geometric. Recognizing the right distribution lets you apply pre-computed formulas, simulate scenarios, and compute probabilities without re-deriving everything. The DataCamp Data Scientist Associate exam tests recognizing which distribution applies, computing PMF values, and using scipy.stats.

Discrete vs continuous

DISCRETE DISTRIBUTIONS
Take countable values (0, 1, 2, ...) — typically COUNTS or YES/NO outcomes.

Described by a PMF (probability mass function): P(X = k) for each possible k.
Probabilities sum to 1 across all possible values.

Bernoulli — one trial, success or failure

BERNOULLI(p)
Models a single yes/no trial with success probability p.

X = 1 if success (probability p)
X = 0 if failure (probability 1 − p)

E[X] = p    Var(X) = p(1 − p)    SD(X) = √[p(1−p)] 
from scipy import stats

# Single coin flip with p = 0.5
X = stats.bernoulli(p=0.5)
X.pmf(0) # 0.5 — P(tail)
X.pmf(1) # 0.5 — P(head)
X.mean() # 0.5
X.var() # 0.25
X.rvs(size=10) # 10 samples — array of 0s and 1s

# Biased coin: p = 0.7
X = stats.bernoulli(p=0.7)
X.mean() # 0.7
X.var() # 0.21

Examples: a single coin flip, a single user converting on your site, a single survey respondent picking "yes," a single email being spam.

Binomial — count of successes in n independent trials

BINOMIAL(n, p)
Sum of n independent Bernoulli(p) trials.
X = number of successes in n trials.

P(X = k) = C(n, k) × p^k × (1−p)^(n−k)

E[X] = np    Var(X) = np(1 − p)

When to recognize: "n trials, each independent, each with same success probability, count of successes." 
from scipy import stats

# 10 coin flips, count heads
X = stats.binom(n=10, p=0.5)
X.pmf(5) # P(exactly 5 heads) ≈ 0.246
X.cdf(5) # P(at most 5 heads) ≈ 0.623
1 - X.cdf(5) # P(more than 5 heads) ≈ 0.377
X.sf(5) # same as 1-cdf, often more precise — "survival function"
X.mean() # 5.0
X.var() # 2.5

# Practical: 100 users see an ad, conversion rate = 0.03
# Probability of getting more than 5 conversions?
X = stats.binom(n=100, p=0.03)
P_more_than_5 = X.sf(5) # ≈ 0.084
P_exactly_3 = X.pmf(3) # ≈ 0.227
X.mean() # 3.0 — expected conversions

# Generate 1000 simulated experiments
samples = X.rvs(size=1000) # array of counts

When binomial conditions actually hold

★ BINOMIAL CHECKLIST — BINS
  • Binary outcomes (success or failure, two categories)
  • Independent trials (one trial's outcome doesn't affect the next)
  • N fixed in advance (you decided to do n trials)
  • Same probability p across trials

If any of these fail, binomial isn't the right model.

Common binomial mis-applications

  • "Sampling without replacement" from a finite population — trials aren't independent. Use hypergeometric. (But binomial is fine as an approximation when sample is <10% of population.)
  • Conversion rate changes during the experiment — p isn't constant.
  • Users come from clustered traffic — same person counted twice, breaking independence.

Poisson — count of rare events in fixed time/space

POISSON(λ)
Counts how many times an event occurs in a fixed interval when events occur INDEPENDENTLY at a constant average RATE λ.

P(X = k) = (e^−λ × λ^k) / k!

E[X] = λ    Var(X) = λ    (mean = variance — a Poisson signature)

Examples: customers per hour, defects per batch, deaths-by-horse-kick per regiment-year (the original 1898 dataset). 
from scipy import stats

# Call center receives an average of 4 calls per hour
X = stats.poisson(mu=4)
X.pmf(0) # P(no calls) = e^-4 ≈ 0.0183
X.pmf(4) # P(exactly 4) ≈ 0.195
X.cdf(2) # P(2 or fewer) ≈ 0.238
X.sf(6) # P(more than 6) ≈ 0.111
X.mean() # 4.0 — by definition equals λ
X.var() # 4.0 — also equals λ

# How many calls in an 8-hour shift?
# If rate is 4/hour, total expected in 8 hours = 32
X = stats.poisson(mu=32)
X.pmf(30) # ≈ 0.0683
X.sf(50) # P(more than 50 calls in shift) ≈ 0.00097

# Sample experiment 1000 times
samples = X.rvs(size=1000)
samples.mean() # ≈ 32 with some variance

Poisson assumptions

  • Events independent (one event doesn't trigger or prevent another)
  • Constant rate (no time-of-day or seasonality effects within the interval)
  • No two events at exactly the same instant (good for rare events)
⚠ POISSON OVERDISPERSION

Real-world count data often has variance > mean — overdispersion. This violates the Poisson assumption.

Common cause: events cluster (e.g., earthquakes trigger aftershocks; viral posts trigger more views).

When variance > mean, switch to the negative binomial distribution.

Poisson approximation to binomial

# When n is large and p is small (rare events), Poisson ≈ Binomial
# With λ = np

# Example: 10000 emails, P(spam) = 0.001
# Binomial(n=10000, p=0.001)
# Poisson(mu = 10000 * 0.001 = 10) — same expected count, simpler formula

binom = stats.binom(n=10000, p=0.001).pmf(15) # P(exactly 15 spam)
poiss = stats.poisson(mu=10).pmf(15) # approximation
# Differences are tiny — typically < 1%

# Rule of thumb: n ≥ 100, p ≤ 0.05, np ≤ 10 — Poisson is a great approximation

Geometric — trials until first success

GEOMETRIC(p)
Counts trials until the first success, in a series of independent Bernoulli(p) trials.

P(X = k) = (1 − p)^(k−1) × p

(scipy uses k = 1, 2, 3, ... — number of trials including the success)

E[X] = 1/p    Var(X) = (1 − p)/p²

Two conventions exist: "trials until first success" (k ≥ 1) and "failures before first success" (k ≥ 0). Scipy uses the first. 
from scipy import stats

# Roll a fair die — number of rolls until you get a 6
X = stats.geom(p=1/6)
X.pmf(1) # P(first roll is a 6) = 1/6 ≈ 0.167
X.pmf(3) # P(first 6 on third roll) = (5/6)² × 1/6 ≈ 0.116
X.cdf(10) # P(first 6 within 10 rolls) ≈ 0.838
X.mean() # 6.0 — average rolls to see a 6
X.var() # 30.0

# Memoryless property of geometric:
# P(X > a + b | X > a) = P(X > b)
# "If you haven't rolled a 6 in 10 tries, the future doesn't care about that history"

# Sales calls — closing rate is 10%. Expected calls to first close?
X = stats.geom(p=0.10)
X.mean() # 10 — 10 calls on average
X.cdf(20) # P(closed within 20 calls) ≈ 0.878

Negative binomial — generalization

# Negative binomial: trials until the r-th success
# Geometric is the special case r = 1

from scipy.stats import nbinom

# Number of failures before 3rd success, with p=0.4
# scipy parameterization: nbinom(n=r, p=p) counts FAILURES, not total trials
X = nbinom(n=3, p=0.4)
X.pmf(5) # P(exactly 5 failures before 3rd success)
X.mean() # r * (1-p) / p = 3 * 0.6 / 0.4 = 4.5 failures expected

# Negative binomial is also commonly used for OVERDISPERSED count data
# Useful when Poisson assumption fails because variance > mean

Identification flowchart

★ WHICH DISCRETE DISTRIBUTION FITS?
  1. Is it ONE binary trial? → Bernoulli
  2. Is it a fixed number of trials, counting successes? → Binomial
  3. Is it a count over an interval, no fixed n? → Poisson
  4. Is it "how many trials until first success"? → Geometric
  5. Is it "how many trials until the r-th success"? → Negative Binomial

Worked example — recognizing the right distribution

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE

Scenario: You're analyzing a help-desk system.

QUESTION 1: "What's the chance the next caller's issue is urgent?"
 → ONE trial, two outcomes (urgent or not)
 → Bernoulli(p), where p is the empirical urgent rate

QUESTION 2: "Of the 50 calls today, how many will be urgent?"
 → 50 independent trials, count of successes
 → Binomial(n=50, p=urgent_rate)

QUESTION 3: "How many calls will come in the next hour?"
 → Count over a fixed time interval, random arrivals
 → Poisson(λ = avg_calls_per_hour)

QUESTION 4: "How many calls until we get an urgent one?"
 → Trials until first success
 → Geometric(p=urgent_rate)

# Code for question 2 — what's the chance of 5+ urgent in 50 calls (urgent rate 8%)?
from scipy import stats
X = stats.binom(n=50, p=0.08)
print(f"P(5 or more urgent) = {X.sf(4):.3f}") # sf(4) = P(X > 4) = P(X ≥ 5)
# About 0.376

# Code for question 3 — what's the chance of 10+ calls in an hour (avg 6/hr)?
Y = stats.poisson(mu=6)
print(f"P(10 or more calls) = {Y.sf(9):.3f}")
# About 0.084

Simulating discrete distributions

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# Simulation is great for verifying analytical answers and exploring complex scenarios

# Binomial — 1000 simulated experiments
trials = stats.binom(n=10, p=0.5).rvs(size=10000)
# Estimate P(X >= 7)
prob_estimate = (trials >= 7).mean() # ≈ 0.172
analytical = stats.binom(n=10, p=0.5).sf(6)
# Should be very close

# Poisson
arrivals = stats.poisson(mu=4).rvs(size=10000)
# Average arrivals
arrivals.mean() # ≈ 4.0

# Visualization — plot empirical vs theoretical PMF
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
samples = stats.binom(n=10, p=0.5).rvs(size=10000)
plt.hist(samples, bins=range(12), density=True, alpha=0.6, label='Empirical')
k = np.arange(0, 11)
plt.plot(k, stats.binom(n=10, p=0.5).pmf(k), 'o-', label='Theoretical PMF')
plt.legend(); plt.xlabel('k'); plt.ylabel('Probability')
plt.show()
# Empirical bars should align with the theoretical line

Common discrete-distribution bugs

⚠ TYPICAL MISTAKES
  1. Applying binomial without independence (clustered users, sequential dependence)
  2. Using Poisson with overdispersion — variance > mean violates Poisson; use negative binomial
  3. Confusing geometric conventions — "trials until success" (k ≥ 1) vs "failures before success" (k ≥ 0)
  4. Forgetting cdf vs pmf vs sf: pmf is P(X=k); cdf is P(X≤k); sf is P(X>k) = 1 − cdf
  5. Off-by-one with sf: P(X ≥ 5) is sf(4), not sf(5)
  6. Poisson with non-constant rate — time-varying λ requires nonhomogeneous Poisson process
  7. Sampling without replacement from small populations — use hypergeometric, not binomial
  8. Assuming p is known when it's estimated — confidence intervals on p change downstream answers
★ ON THE EXAM

"Bernoulli E[X]?" → p; Var(X) = p(1−p).

"Binomial E[X]?" → np; Var(X) = np(1−p).

"Poisson E[X]?" → λ; Var(X) = λ (mean equals variance).

"Geometric E[X]?" → 1/p (using "trials until success" convention).

"Count of yes/no successes in fixed n trials?" → Binomial.

"Count of rare events in fixed time?" → Poisson.

"Trials until first success?" → Geometric.

"Poisson approximation to binomial?" → Valid when n is large, p small (np ≤ 10).

"P(X ≥ k) with scipy?" → dist.sf(k-1) (off by one!) or 1 - dist.cdf(k-1).

"PMF vs CDF?" → PMF is P(X=k) at a point; CDF is P(X≤k) cumulative.

"Mean of Poisson = variance?" → Yes — defining property; if variance > mean in data, use negative binomial.

"Binomial BINS check?" → Binary, Independent, N fixed, Same probability.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Discrete distributions describe count-valued random variables via their PMF
  • Bernoulli: a single success/failure trial; E[X] = p, Var = p(1−p)
  • Binomial: count of successes in n independent Bernoulli trials; E[X] = np, Var = np(1−p)
  • BINS check for binomial: Binary, Independent, N fixed, Same probability
  • Poisson: count of independent rare events at constant rate λ in fixed interval; E[X] = Var(X) = λ
  • Poisson approximates binomial well when n is large, p is small, np ≤ 10
  • Overdispersion (variance > mean) violates Poisson — use negative binomial instead
  • Geometric: trials until first success; E[X] = 1/p, Var = (1−p)/p²
  • Geometric is memoryless — past failures don't change future probabilities
  • scipy.stats: bernoulli, binom, poisson, geom, nbinom — all have .pmf, .cdf, .sf, .rvs
  • P(X ≥ k) = sf(k-1), not sf(k) — the off-by-one trap
  • Simulate with .rvs(size=n) to verify analytical answers
  • Identifying the right distribution is the most-tested skill: count vs first-success vs binary vs interval-rate
📊 FIGURE — A binomial distribution: Bin(10, 0.5)
Ten independent yes/no trials: the bar at k is P(exactly k successes) = C(10,k)p^k(1−p)^(10−k). Symmetric here because p = ½, peaked at np = 5. Poisson handles rare-event counts; geometric waits for the first success.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The normal distribution alone underlies a huge fraction of all statistical methods — confidence intervals, t-tests, regression, neural network initializations. Uniform models pure randomness; exponential models waiting times. Together they cover most continuous data you'll encounter on the DataCamp Data Scientist Associate exam, plus most real-world modeling.

Continuous vs discrete — a critical distinction

CONTINUOUS DISTRIBUTIONS
Take values in a real interval (not just integers).

Described by a PDF (probability density function) f(x).
P(X = exact value) = 0 — for continuous RVs, only ranges have positive probability.

P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx — the area under the PDF.
Total area under PDF = 1. 
# For a continuous RV X:
# P(X = 5) = 0 ← always, regardless of distribution
# P(4.99 ≤ X ≤ 5.01) > 0 ← positive

# To compute probabilities, use the CDF (cumulative distribution function):
# P(X ≤ x) = CDF(x)
# P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = CDF(b) - CDF(a)

# This is different from discrete, where P(X = k) is meaningful

The Normal (Gaussian) distribution

NORMAL(μ, σ²)
The famous bell curve. Two parameters: mean μ and variance σ² (or standard deviation σ).

E[X] = μ    Var(X) = σ²

Symmetric around μ. Approximately 68%/95%/99.7% within 1/2/3 standard deviations.

Arises naturally for sums/averages of many independent factors (CLT — section s4). 
from scipy import stats

# Standard normal — mean 0, SD 1
Z = stats.norm()
Z.pdf(0) # density at 0 — ≈ 0.399 (peak height)
Z.cdf(0) # P(Z ≤ 0) = 0.5 (symmetric)
Z.cdf(1.96) # P(Z ≤ 1.96) ≈ 0.975
Z.sf(1.96) # P(Z > 1.96) ≈ 0.025
Z.ppf(0.975) # inverse CDF: which value has P(Z ≤ x) = 0.975? → 1.96
Z.rvs(size=10) # 10 random samples

# General normal with mean μ and SD σ
X = stats.norm(loc=100, scale=15) # IQ-like distribution
X.cdf(115) # P(IQ ≤ 115) ≈ 0.841
X.sf(130) # P(IQ > 130) ≈ 0.023
X.ppf(0.95) # 95th percentile ≈ 124.7

# Probability that IQ is between 85 and 115
P_within_1sd = X.cdf(115) - X.cdf(85) # ≈ 0.683 (the 68% rule)

The 68/95/99.7 rule

★ THE EMPIRICAL RULE

For an approximately normal distribution with mean μ and SD σ:

  • ≈ 68% of values lie within μ ± 1σ
  • ≈ 95% within μ ± 2σ (more precisely 1.96 σ)
  • ≈ 99.7% within μ ± 3σ

Memorize these — they're the foundation of confidence intervals and rough mental computations on normal data.

Why the normal distribution is everywhere

  • Central Limit Theorem — averages of independent samples are approximately normal (covered in s4)
  • Sums of many small independent random effects tend to be normal (heights, measurement errors)
  • Logarithms of multiplicative processes (incomes, stock returns) are often approximately normal
  • Mathematically tractable — closed-form formulas, easy to combine

Uniform distribution — pure randomness within bounds

UNIFORM(a, b) — CONTINUOUS
Every value in [a, b] equally likely.

PDF: f(x) = 1/(b−a) on [a, b], 0 elsewhere

E[X] = (a + b)/2    Var(X) = (b − a)²/12

The "background noise" of probability — a random number generator's output before transformation. 
from scipy import stats

# Uniform on [0, 1] — what numpy's random() returns
X = stats.uniform(loc=0, scale=1) # scale = b - a
X.cdf(0.3) # 0.3 — P(X ≤ 0.3) is just 0.3
X.mean() # 0.5
X.var() # 1/12 ≈ 0.0833

# Uniform on [10, 30]
X = stats.uniform(loc=10, scale=20) # loc = a, scale = b - a
X.cdf(20) # P(X ≤ 20) = (20-10)/(30-10) = 0.5
X.mean() # 20

# Common uses:
# • Modeling things truly random within bounds (a roll of an infinitely-faceted die)
# • Generating random samples to test other distributions
# • Bootstrap resampling and random-number generation seeds

Inverse-CDF (probability integral) trick

# Universal way to generate samples from ANY distribution:
# 1. Generate U ~ Uniform(0, 1)
# 2. Apply the inverse CDF of your target distribution

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# Generate samples from a normal using only uniforms
u = np.random.uniform(0, 1, 10000)
normal_samples = stats.norm.ppf(u)
# normal_samples now ~ Normal(0, 1)

# Why does this work?
# If U is uniform, then F^(-1)(U) follows the distribution with CDF F.

# This is how all random number generators work internally for non-uniform distributions.

Exponential distribution — waiting times

EXPONENTIAL(λ) — OR EXPONENTIAL(1/λ) in scipy
Time until the next event in a Poisson process (events at rate λ per unit time).

PDF: f(x) = λ × e^(−λx) for x ≥ 0

E[X] = 1/λ    Var(X) = 1/λ²

scipy parameterization: stats.expon(scale=1/λ) — scipy uses the MEAN as scale.

Memoryless: P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t) — like geometric for continuous time. 
from scipy import stats

# Calls arrive at 4 per hour → mean time between calls = 0.25 hours = 15 minutes
# scipy scale = mean = 0.25 hours
X = stats.expon(scale=0.25) # NOT scale=4!

X.cdf(0.5) # P(next call within 30 min) ≈ 0.865
X.sf(1.0) # P(no call for 1 hour) ≈ 0.0183
X.mean() # 0.25 hours
X.median() # ln(2)/λ ≈ 0.173 — median is shorter than mean (right-skewed)

# Examples:
# • Time between customer arrivals
# • Lifetime of electronic components with constant failure rate
# • Time between earthquakes (controversial — there's some clustering)
# • Duration until next server request

# Connection to Poisson:
# If event count over time is Poisson(λt), inter-arrival times are Exponential(λ)
# Two views of the same underlying process

The memoryless property in practice

# "Memoryless" = the distribution of remaining waiting time
# doesn't depend on how long you've already waited.

# Example: customer arrivals
# E[next call] = 15 min from now, regardless of when last call was
# You've been waiting 20 min already? Still 15 min expected from now.
# This is what makes exponential the natural "no memory" continuous waiting time

# Counterintuitive — most real waiting feels NOT memoryless:
# Waiting 20 minutes for a bus that runs every 15 minutes feels like it's "due"
# But that's because actual bus arrivals AREN'T exponential — they have a schedule

Other useful continuous distributions

Log-normal

# If log(X) is normal, X is log-normal
# Right-skewed; common for incomes, stock prices, file sizes
X = stats.lognorm(s=0.5) # s is the SD of log(X)

# To fit: take log of data, then fit normal
import numpy as np
log_incomes = np.log(incomes)
mu, sigma = log_incomes.mean(), log_incomes.std(ddof=1)
fitted = stats.lognorm(s=sigma, scale=np.exp(mu))

Gamma — generalization of exponential

# Gamma(k, θ) — waiting time for k events in a Poisson process
# Exponential is Gamma(k=1)
# E[X] = kθ, Var(X) = kθ²

X = stats.gamma(a=3, scale=2)
# Models: total claim amounts, rainfall amounts, server load metrics

Beta — distribution over probabilities

# Beta(α, β) — distribution on [0, 1]
# Models proportions, rates, click-through rates, conversion rates
# Used as a PRIOR over a probability in Bayesian inference (conjugate to binomial)

X = stats.beta(a=2, b=5)
X.mean() # 2 / (2+5) = 0.286
# As α gets larger, distribution shifts right (toward 1)
# As β gets larger, shifts left (toward 0)
# Special case: Beta(1, 1) = Uniform(0, 1)

Working with PDFs and CDFs in code

from scipy import stats
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Common methods on any scipy distribution object
X = stats.norm(loc=100, scale=15)

X.pdf(110) # density at a point
X.cdf(110) # P(X ≤ 110)
X.sf(110) # P(X > 110), = 1 - cdf
X.ppf(0.5) # inverse CDF (percentile point function): which x has CDF = 0.5
X.median() # = ppf(0.5)
X.mean() # E[X]
X.var() # Var(X)
X.std() # SD
X.rvs(size=1000) # 1000 random samples

plt.title('Normal(100, 15) PDF')
plt.xlabel('x'); plt.ylabel('density')
plt.show()

Worked example — modeling service times

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Service-time analysis

Scenario: Customer service calls last on average 8 minutes. You want to know:

  1. What's the chance a call lasts more than 15 minutes?
  2. What's the chance it ends within 5 minutes?
  3. How long must we plan for to capture 95% of calls?
from scipy import stats

# Assume exponential — constant termination rate (idealized)
# Mean = 8 minutes, so scale = 8 (NOT λ = 1/8!)
X = stats.expon(scale=8)

# Q1: P(call > 15 min)
p_long = X.sf(15) # ≈ 0.153

# Q2: P(call ≤ 5 min)
p_short = X.cdf(5) # ≈ 0.465

# Q3: 95th percentile
p95 = X.ppf(0.95) # ≈ 23.97 min — plan for ~24 min coverage

# Compare to NORMAL with same mean and SD (≈ 8 for exponential)
N = stats.norm(loc=8, scale=8)
N.sf(15) # ≈ 0.191 — different, because normal has lighter tails
N.ppf(0.95) # ≈ 21.16 — different 95th %ile

# Picking the right model matters — exponential has a heavier right tail
# Always check if your data is approximately exponential before using formulas

Recognizing distributions in real data

★ HOW TO PICK A DISTRIBUTION FROM DATA
  1. Look at the histogram — symmetric bell? Normal. Right-skewed with positive support? Exponential or log-normal. Flat? Uniform.
  2. Look at the support — only positive? Rules out normal. On [0,1]? Beta is a candidate.
  3. Compare mean vs median — if equal, symmetric (normal-like). If mean > median, right-skewed (log-normal, exponential).
  4. Check Q-Q plot — points on the line = good fit to that distribution.
  5. Goodness-of-fit tests — Kolmogorov-Smirnov (stats.kstest), Anderson-Darling, Shapiro-Wilk for normality.

Common continuous-distribution bugs

⚠ TYPICAL MISTAKES
  1. Treating P(X = x) as positive for continuous data — it's always 0; only ranges matter
  2. scipy.stats.expon scale confusion — scale = MEAN = 1/λ, NOT λ
  3. Using normal for data with hard bounds — heights can't be negative; consider log-normal or truncated normal
  4. Misreading scipy's loc and scale — for uniform, loc = a and scale = b−a (not b)
  5. Confusing PDF with probability — PDF values can exceed 1; only INTEGRAL of PDF is a probability
  6. Assuming normality without checking — many real datasets aren't normal; methods relying on normality may give wrong answers
  7. Using mean and SD on heavy-tailed data — for log-normal, exponential, etc., median and IQR are more meaningful
  8. Treating PDF as P(X near x) — to get a probability, multiply by a small width or integrate
★ ON THE EXAM

"P(X = exact value) for continuous X?" → 0 (always).

"P(a ≤ X ≤ b) =?" → CDF(b) − CDF(a).

"Normal 68/95/99.7 rule?" → ~68% within 1 SD, ~95% within 2 SD (1.96), ~99.7% within 3 SD.

"Find 97.5th percentile of standard normal?" → ≈ 1.96 (use norm.ppf(0.975)).

"Z-score = 1.96 corresponds to?" → P(Z > 1.96) ≈ 0.025; two-tailed: 95% CI.

"scipy expon(scale=X) — what is scale?" → The MEAN (1/λ).

"Memoryless distributions?" → Geometric (discrete) and Exponential (continuous).

"PDF height at a point?" → A density, not a probability — can exceed 1.

"Distribution with E[X] = Var(X)?" → Poisson (discrete) or Exponential (with appropriate parameterization).

"Sum of normals is?" → Also normal. Sum of independent normals: mean adds, variances add.

"Recognize a normal-looking dataset?" → Symmetric bell, mean ≈ median, ~68% within 1 SD.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Continuous distributions use a PDF, not PMF; P(X = exact value) = 0 always
  • Compute probabilities from the CDF: P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = CDF(b) − CDF(a)
  • PDF values can exceed 1 — they're densities, not probabilities; only integrals are probabilities
  • Normal(μ, σ²): the bell curve; 68/95/99.7 within 1/2/3 SDs of the mean
  • Standard normal is Normal(0, 1); used to compute z-scores
  • Uniform(a, b): every value in [a, b] equally likely; mean = (a+b)/2; var = (b−a)²/12
  • Exponential(λ): time until next event in Poisson process; memoryless; right-skewed
  • scipy.stats.expon uses scale = MEAN, not λ — common bug
  • scipy methods: .pdf, .cdf, .sf, .ppf (inverse CDF), .rvs, .mean, .var
  • Log-normal: log of a normal; common for income, prices, anything multiplicative
  • Beta: distribution on [0, 1]; common for probabilities and proportions
  • Inverse-CDF trick lets you sample any distribution from uniform inputs
  • Always check distributional assumptions on your data via histogram + Q-Q plot before using formulas
📊 FIGURE — Three continuous shapes to recognize on sight
Uniform: every value in [a, b] equally likely — a flat block. Normal: the symmetric bell from summed effects. Exponential: waiting times — most mass near zero, a long right tail, and the memoryless property.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The standard normal distribution is the workhorse of statistics. Every confidence interval, every t-test, every hypothesis test eventually converts to a z-score or a related statistic and looks up a probability. The 1.96 you see everywhere comes from here. The DataCamp Data Scientist Associate exam tests z-score computation, looking up probabilities, and the inverse direction (probability → value).

What "standard" means

STANDARD NORMAL — N(0, 1)
Mean μ = 0, variance σ² = 1, standard deviation σ = 1.

Universally denoted Z (to distinguish from a general normal X).
All other normal distributions can be transformed to Z and back via the z-score. 
from scipy import stats

Z = stats.norm() # default loc=0, scale=1 — standard normal
Z.cdf(0) # 0.5 (the median is 0)
Z.cdf(1) # 0.841 (P(Z ≤ 1))
Z.cdf(-1) # 0.159 (P(Z ≤ -1))
Z.cdf(1) - Z.cdf(-1) # 0.683 (the 68% rule)

# Common critical values to memorize:
Z.ppf(0.5) # 0.0 median
Z.ppf(0.95) # 1.645 one-tailed 95%
Z.ppf(0.975) # 1.960 two-tailed 95% (most-cited number in stats)
Z.ppf(0.99) # 2.326 one-tailed 99%
Z.ppf(0.995) # 2.576 two-tailed 99%

Z-score — standardizing any value

Z-SCORE
For X ~ Normal(μ, σ²):

z = (x − μ) / σ

Interpretation: "how many standard deviations is x above (or below) the mean?"
After this transformation, Z ~ Normal(0, 1). 
# IQ scores: Normal(100, 15²)
# Someone scores 130. What's their z-score?
mu, sigma = 100, 15
x = 130
z = (x - mu) / sigma # 2.0 — two standard deviations above mean

# What's their percentile?
from scipy import stats
percentile = stats.norm.cdf(z) # 0.9772 — better than 97.7% of people

# Equivalent without computing z first:
percentile = stats.norm(loc=100, scale=15).cdf(130)
# Same answer — the cdf method does the z transformation internally

Z-scores translate everything to a common scale

# Two students' test scores:
# Alice — SAT: 1400 (mean 1000, SD 200)
# Bob — ACT: 28 (mean 21, SD 5)
# Who did better RELATIVE to their test?

z_alice = (1400 - 1000) / 200 # 2.0
z_bob = (28 - 21) / 5 # 1.4
# Alice's z is higher → Alice scored better relative to her test takers

# Same logic to compare:
# • Heights across populations with different averages
# • Salaries across industries with different scales
# • Anything where the question is "how exceptional?"

Going from probability to z (the inverse)

# Often phrased: "what value separates the top X%?"
# Answer: find the z value, then convert back

# What IQ separates the top 1%?
top_1pct_z = stats.norm.ppf(0.99) # 2.326
iq_threshold = 100 + 2.326 * 15 # ≈ 134.9

# What's the 25th percentile of birth weights with mean 3.5kg, SD 0.5kg?
z25 = stats.norm.ppf(0.25) # -0.674
weight_25th = 3.5 + (-0.674) * 0.5 # ≈ 3.16 kg

# What weight is exceeded by exactly 5% of newborns?
# Top 5% → 95th percentile
z95 = stats.norm.ppf(0.95) # 1.645
weight = 3.5 + 1.645 * 0.5 # ≈ 4.32 kg

# General formula
x = mu + z * sigma

Two-tailed probabilities — symmetric ranges

# "Find values cutting off the middle 95% of the distribution"
# Equivalent to "values within ±z standard deviations"

z = stats.norm.ppf(0.975) # 1.96 (since 2.5% in EACH tail leaves 95% in middle)

# So for IQ:
lower = 100 - 1.96 * 15 # ≈ 70.6
upper = 100 + 1.96 * 15 # ≈ 129.4
# 95% of people have IQ between 70.6 and 129.4

# Common cutoffs:
# 90% middle → z = 1.645
# 95% middle → z = 1.96
# 99% middle → z = 2.576

# Verify by checking P(-1.96 ≤ Z ≤ 1.96)
stats.norm.cdf(1.96) - stats.norm.cdf(-1.96) # ≈ 0.95 ✓

Tails of the standard normal — common probabilities

z valueP(Z ≤ z)P(Z > z) (one tail)P(|Z| > z) (two tails)

★ MEMORIZE THESE
  • z = 1.96 → 95% middle, 2.5% in each tail (most common!)
  • z = 1.645 → 90% middle / 5% one tail
  • z = 2.576 → 99% middle
  • z = 3 → ~99.7% middle (the "three sigma" rule)

The 1.96 in particular shows up in every confidence interval you'll see. It's worth memorizing exactly.

Standardizing entire datasets

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# Manual z-score
data = np.array([85, 90, 78, 92, 88, 76, 95])
z_scores = (data - data.mean()) / data.std(ddof=1)
# Standardized: mean 0, SD 1

# scipy
from scipy import stats
z_scores = stats.zscore(data, ddof=1)

# pandas
df['z_score'] = (df['value'] - df['value'].mean()) / df['value'].std()

# Or use sklearn
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X)
# Same operation across each column — mean 0, SD 1 per column

Why standardize before modeling

  • Distance-based algorithms (KNN, k-means, SVM) need features on the same scale
  • Gradient descent converges faster on standardized data
  • Regularized models (Lasso, Ridge) penalize coefficients — must be comparable
  • Comparison across variables — z-score makes "1 SD increase" units comparable
⚠ STANDARDIZE WITH TRAIN STATS, NOT TEST
scaler = StandardScaler()
scaler.fit(X_train) # fit on training data only
X_train_scaled = scaler.transform(X_train)
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test) # use train-fitted parameters!

# DON'T fit_transform on test data — that leaks info from test into normalization

Outlier detection with z-scores

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# Rule of thumb: |z| > 3 might be an outlier (under normal assumption)
z_scores = stats.zscore(data, ddof=1)
outliers = np.abs(z_scores) > 3

# Use case: clean a sensor stream of obvious bad readings
# Caveats:
# 1. Only valid if data is approximately normal
# 2. Mean and SD are themselves pulled by outliers (chicken-egg)
# 3. For skewed data, use IQR-based or modified z-score

# Modified z-score (more robust)
def modified_zscore(data):
 median = np.median(data)
 mad = np.median(np.abs(data - median)) # median absolute deviation
 return 0.6745 * (data - median) / mad # 0.6745 makes it comparable to standard z
# Flag |modified_z| > 3.5 as outliers

Worked example — using z-scores in practice

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Hiring threshold

Scenario: Test scores on your hiring exam have mean 75 and SD 10 (approximately normal). Your hiring policy:

  • Auto-pass: top 10% of scores
  • Auto-fail: bottom 25%
  • Review: everyone in between

What score thresholds correspond?

from scipy import stats

mu, sigma = 75, 10

# Top 10% means scores above the 90th percentile
z_pass = stats.norm.ppf(0.90) # 1.282
pass_score = mu + z_pass * sigma # 75 + 12.82 = 87.82
# Anyone scoring 88+ auto-passes

# Bottom 25% means below the 25th percentile
z_fail = stats.norm.ppf(0.25) # -0.674
fail_score = mu + z_fail * sigma # 75 - 6.74 = 68.26
# Anyone scoring 68 or below auto-fails

# Manual review for scores between 68 and 88

# Suppose a candidate scores 90. How exceptional?
z = (90 - mu) / sigma # 1.5
percentile = stats.norm.cdf(z) # 0.9332
# 93rd percentile — top 7% of test-takers

The Q-Q plot — checking normality with z-scores

import scipy.stats as stats
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Q-Q plot compares sample quantiles to theoretical normal quantiles
stats.probplot(data, dist='norm', plot=plt)
plt.title('Q-Q Plot vs Normal')
plt.show()

# Points fall on the line → data is approximately normal
# Concave up → left-skewed
# Concave down → right-skewed
# S-shaped → heavier tails than normal
# Reverse-S → lighter tails

# Formal normality tests:
stats.shapiro(data) # Shapiro-Wilk (best for n < 50)
stats.normaltest(data) # D'Agostino-Pearson (good general purpose)
stats.kstest(data, 'norm') # Kolmogorov-Smirnov

# Caveat: with very large n, these reject normality even for tiny deviations
# Always also visually check the Q-Q plot

Common z-score / standard normal bugs

⚠ TYPICAL MISTAKES
  1. Confusing one-tailed and two-tailed cutoffs — for 95% middle, use 1.96 (two-tailed); for 95% one-tailed, use 1.645
  2. Sign errors — left-tail probabilities are not 1 − right-tail in z = 0 directions; always be explicit
  3. Forgetting that ppf is the INVERSE of cdf — ppf(0.975) = 1.96 because cdf(1.96) = 0.975
  4. Standardizing with test-set statistics — leaks information; always use training mean/SD
  5. Treating z > 3 outliers without verifying normality — non-normal data has different tail probabilities
  6. Confusing standard NORMAL (continuous distribution) with standardized data — they're related but different concepts
  7. Using sample SD when population SD is given (or vice versa) — different formulas in inference
  8. Off-by-one with percentile interpretation — "top 5%" means 95th percentile, not 5th
★ ON THE EXAM

"Standard normal parameters?" → mean 0, SD 1.

"Z-score formula?" → (x − μ) / σ.

"Z = 1.96 corresponds to?" → P(Z > 1.96) ≈ 0.025; 95% of probability in (-1.96, 1.96).

"P(Z < 0)?" → 0.5 (Z is symmetric around 0).

"Find the value at the 95th percentile of N(μ, σ²)?" → μ + 1.645σ.

"Find the value at the 97.5th percentile?" → μ + 1.96σ.

"68/95/99.7 rule values?" → within ±1, ±1.96, ±3 standard deviations.

"Why standardize features for ML?" → Distance-based methods (KNN), gradient descent convergence, regularization.

"Modified z-score?" → 0.6745 × (x − median) / MAD. More robust than standard z-score.

"Q-Q plot?" → Compares sample quantiles to theoretical (typically normal) quantiles.

"Sample standardization in sklearn?" → StandardScaler() — fit on train, transform on test.

"95% middle of N(μ, σ²)?" → μ ± 1.96σ.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Standard normal Z ~ N(0, 1) has mean 0 and SD 1
  • Z-score: z = (x − μ) / σ — how many SDs x is from the mean
  • Any normal can be standardized via z-score, then looked up against Z's CDF
  • 1.96 cuts off the middle 95% of standard normal (97.5th percentile); 1.645 the 95th
  • For 99% middle, use 2.576; for 99.7%, use 3
  • scipy's norm.cdf(z) gives P(Z ≤ z); norm.ppf(p) goes the other way
  • To compute x from a percentile: x = μ + z × σ
  • Z-scores let you compare values across different scales (test scores, salaries, heights)
  • StandardScaler in sklearn does z-scoring per column; always fit on TRAIN only, transform TEST
  • |z| > 3 outlier rule applies only to approximately normal data — use modified z-score (with MAD) for robust detection
  • Q-Q plot visually tests if data is approximately normal — points on the line = good fit
  • Memorize 1.96 (= 97.5th percentile, two-tailed 95% CI) — it appears in nearly every confidence interval
📊 FIGURE — The normal curve and the 68–95–99.7 rule
For any normal distribution: about 68% of values fall within 1 standard deviation of the mean, 95% within 2, and 99.7% within 3. Z-scores just measure position in σ-units: z = (x − μ)/σ, so "z = 2" always means "2σ above the mean" regardless of the original units.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The Central Limit Theorem (CLT) is the most important result in statistics. It says that averages of independent samples become approximately normal — no matter what the underlying distribution looks like. This single fact is why confidence intervals, t-tests, A/B testing, polling, and most of modern statistics works. The DataCamp Data Scientist Associate exam tests CLT recognition, sampling-distribution standard error, and conditions for applicability.

Statistic vs parameter — the population/sample distinction

TermMeaningSymbol
ParameterA fixed (usually unknown) number describing the POPULATIONμ, σ, p
StatisticA number computed from a SAMPLE; varies sample to samplex̄, s, p̂
Sampling distributionThe distribution of a statistic over many possible samples(no single symbol)
 
# Imagine we want to know the average height of all adults in a country.
# μ = the TRUE population average (a fixed number, but unknown to us)

# We take a sample of 100 adults and compute the sample mean x̄.
# x̄ is a STATISTIC. Different samples → different x̄.
# The DISTRIBUTION of x̄ across all possible samples is the sampling distribution.

# Each sample's x̄ is an ESTIMATE of μ.
# We want to know: how close is x̄ likely to be to μ?
# Answer: depends on the sampling distribution of x̄.

The Central Limit Theorem — the headline result

CLT FOR THE SAMPLE MEAN
Let X₁, X₂, ..., Xₙ be iid (independent, identically distributed) random variables with mean μ and finite variance σ². Then as n grows:

x̄ = (X₁ + X₂ + ... + Xₙ) / n   ~   Normal(μ, σ²/n)

In words: the sample mean is approximately NORMAL, with mean equal to the population mean and variance equal to σ²/n.

This holds regardless of the shape of the original distribution.
Skewed, multimodal, weird — the sample mean still goes normal.

Standard error — the SD of the sampling distribution

STANDARD ERROR (SE)

SE = σ / √n

The standard deviation of the sample MEAN, NOT the data itself.
Sample size n in the denominator → larger samples have smaller SE.

When σ is unknown (almost always), estimate with sample SD: SE ≈ s / √n. 
import numpy as np

# Imagine a wildly non-normal distribution — say, exponential
# Population mean μ = 5, SD σ = 5
# Single observations: highly skewed, ranging from 0 to large values

# Draw 1000 samples of size 30 and compute each sample's mean
samples = np.random.exponential(scale=5, size=(1000, 30))
sample_means = samples.mean(axis=1)

# Sample means follow a roughly NORMAL distribution centered at 5
sample_means.mean() # ≈ 5.0 (matches μ)
sample_means.std(ddof=1) # ≈ 5 / sqrt(30) ≈ 0.913 (matches SE = σ/√n)

# Confirm normal shape
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.hist(sample_means, bins=30, density=True, alpha=0.6)
# Overlay a normal with the same mean and SE
from scipy import stats
x = np.linspace(2, 8, 100)
plt.plot(x, stats.norm(loc=5, scale=5/np.sqrt(30)).pdf(x), 'r-')
plt.show()
# The histogram tracks the bell curve — even though individual values were exponential

The CLT in action — visualization

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Watch what happens as n grows
sizes = [1, 2, 5, 30, 100]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(15, 3))

for ax, n in zip(axes, sizes):
 # 10,000 samples of size n from exponential (highly skewed)
 samples = np.random.exponential(scale=5, size=(10000, n))
 means = samples.mean(axis=1)
 ax.hist(means, bins=40, density=True)
 ax.set_title(f'n = {n}')
 ax.set_xlim(0, 20)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# n = 1: looks like the original exponential — heavy right skew
# n = 2: still skewed
# n = 5: skew dramatically reduced
# n = 30: looks bell-shaped
# n = 100: indistinguishable from normal

How fast does CLT kick in?

★ THE n ≥ 30 RULE OF THUMB

For most underlying distributions, the sample mean is approximately normal once n ≥ 30. But this depends on shape:

  • Already normal data: any n is fine; x̄ is exactly normal.
  • Mildly skewed: n ≈ 15-30 is plenty.
  • Highly skewed (income, response time): may need n = 100+.
  • Heavy-tailed without finite variance (Cauchy): CLT FAILS — no amount of n helps.

For the DataCamp exam, "n ≥ 30" is the canonical answer when asked when CLT applies.

CLT for proportions — the binomial case

CLT FOR SAMPLE PROPORTION
If you have n independent Bernoulli(p) trials and let p̂ = (count of successes) / n, then for large n:

p̂ ~ Normal(p, p(1−p)/n)

SE(p̂) = √[p(1−p)/n]

Conditions: np ≥ 10 AND n(1−p) ≥ 10 (need enough successes AND failures). 
import numpy as np

# Imagine: true conversion rate p = 0.05, take a sample of 1000 users
# Sample proportion p̂ is approximately Normal(0.05, 0.05*0.95/1000)
# SE = sqrt(0.05 * 0.95 / 1000) ≈ 0.00689

# Simulation
samples = np.random.binomial(n=1000, p=0.05, size=10000) / 1000
samples.mean() # ≈ 0.05
samples.std(ddof=1) # ≈ 0.00689 — matches the formula

# Confirm: np = 50, n(1-p) = 950 — both >> 10, so normal approximation is good

# What if p is very small? p = 0.001, n = 100 → np = 0.1 << 10
# CLT does NOT apply; use exact binomial (or Poisson approximation)

What if σ is unknown? Use t-distribution

★ KNOWN vs UNKNOWN σ — the t comes in

When you know the true population standard deviation σ, the standardized mean is exactly normal:

Z = (x̄ − μ) / (σ / √n) ~ N(0, 1)

But σ is almost never known. Substituting sample SD s:

T = (x̄ − μ) / (s / √n) ~ t-distribution with (n − 1) degrees of freedom

The t-distribution looks like the normal but with HEAVIER TAILS to account for the extra uncertainty in estimating σ. As n grows, t → Normal.

from scipy import stats

# t-distribution with 10 degrees of freedom
T = stats.t(df=10)
T.ppf(0.975) # 2.228 — heavier tails than 1.96

# Bigger df → closer to normal
stats.t(df=30).ppf(0.975) # 2.042
stats.t(df=100).ppf(0.975) # 1.984
stats.t(df=1000).ppf(0.975) # 1.962 — almost 1.96 (z-value)

# As n → ∞, t → Normal. Often "n ≥ 30 → use z" is a rule of thumb,
# but scipy makes computing t-quantiles painless so just use t for safety.

Distribution of the sample variance — chi-squared

SAMPLE VARIANCE DISTRIBUTION
If X₁, ..., Xₙ ~ Normal(μ, σ²) iid and s² is the sample variance with denominator (n−1):

(n − 1) × s² / σ² ~ χ² with (n − 1) degrees of freedom

Used for confidence intervals on variance and chi-squared goodness-of-fit tests (ch5).

The Law of Large Numbers (LLN) — a different (but related) result

LAW OF LARGE NUMBERS
As n → ∞: x̄ → μ (the sample mean converges to the population mean).

CLT and LLN both say "averages stabilize," but:
  LLN: where the sample mean converges (to μ).
  CLT: how the sample mean fluctuates around μ (normally, scaled by σ/√n). 
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Roll a die many times — running average converges to 3.5 (LLN)
n_max = 10000
rolls = np.random.randint(1, 7, size=n_max)
running_avg = np.cumsum(rolls) / np.arange(1, n_max + 1)

plt.plot(running_avg)
plt.axhline(3.5, color='r', linestyle='--')
plt.xlabel('Trial number')
plt.ylabel('Running average')
plt.show()
# Wobbles a lot early, then settles tightly around 3.5

Why CLT matters — confidence intervals preview

# Without CLT: to make ANY inference about μ from a sample, you'd need to know
# the exact distribution of x̄ for your specific underlying distribution.
# Complicated case-by-case statistics.

# WITH CLT: regardless of underlying distribution, for large n:
# x̄ ~ Normal(μ, σ²/n)
# So:
# 95% of samples have x̄ within μ ± 1.96 × (σ/√n)
# Reversing: μ is in the interval x̄ ± 1.96 × (σ/√n) 95% of the time

# That's the foundation of the 95% confidence interval (next section)

# CLT is why every confidence interval and most hypothesis tests
# use 1.96 (or a similar critical value) — the normal approximation is the backbone

Conditions for CLT — when it works

ConditionWhy it matters
Independent observationsFoundational; correlated data breaks the result. Real-world data often isn't.
Identically distributed (iid)All observations from the same distribution. Generalizations exist for non-iid but use those carefully.
Finite variancePathological distributions (Cauchy) have infinite variance; CLT fails for them.
Sufficient sample sizen ≥ 30 is the rule of thumb; heavily skewed needs more, normal data needs less.
Random samplingOtherwise the sample mean estimates a different quantity than population mean.
⚠ COMMON CLT MISCONCEPTIONS
  • "CLT means the data becomes normal." Wrong. The data stays whatever it was. The DISTRIBUTION OF THE SAMPLE MEAN becomes normal.
  • "You need a normal population for CLT." Wrong. The whole point is that you DON'T — CLT works regardless of the population shape.
  • "CLT lets you use any statistic." Wrong. CLT applies to means and sums, plus quantities that can be expressed in terms of them. Maxima, medians of small samples, etc., need different theory.
  • "n > 30 always works." Wrong. Extremely skewed data may need much larger n.
  • "CLT works for time-series data." Wrong without modification — independence is violated.

Worked example — how big a sample do I need?

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Sample size for precision

Scenario: You want to estimate average customer spend to within ±$5 with 95% confidence. Past data suggests σ ≈ $50.

# Margin of error formula (using normal approximation):
# MOE = 1.96 × σ / √n

# Solve for n:
# n = (1.96 × σ / MOE)²

import math
sigma = 50
moe = 5
z = 1.96

n = (z * sigma / moe) ** 2
n_rounded = math.ceil(n)
# n ≈ 384.16 → round up to 385

# So you need 385+ customers in your sample
# If σ = $100 (more variability), you'd need 4× as many: ~1538
# To get MOE = $2.50 (half), you'd need 4× as many: ~1538

# Key insight: precision scales as 1/√n
# To DOUBLE your precision, you need 4× more data
# To 10× your precision, you need 100× more data

CLT and the bootstrap — modern alternative

# When CLT conditions don't hold, or when you want a statistic other than mean:
# Bootstrap = resampling with replacement from the data itself.

import numpy as np

data = np.array([2, 5, 8, 1, 7, 3, 9, 4, 6, 10])

# Bootstrap distribution of the mean
n_bootstrap = 10000
boot_means = []
for _ in range(n_bootstrap):
 resample = np.random.choice(data, size=len(data), replace=True)
 boot_means.append(resample.mean())

# Use this as the sampling distribution
np.percentile(boot_means, [2.5, 97.5])
# Empirical 95% CI for the mean — no normality assumed

# Bootstrap works for ANY statistic (mean, median, ratio, correlation, ...)
# Especially useful with small samples or weird statistics
# Doesn't replace CLT but extends what you can estimate

Common CLT-related mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Mixing up σ and SE — σ is the spread of one observation; SE = σ/√n is the spread of the sample mean
  2. Forgetting CLT requires independence — repeated measurements on the same subject violate this
  3. Using CLT on the SAMPLE not the SAMPLING DISTRIBUTION — CLT predicts the distribution of x̄, not data
  4. Treating "x̄ is approximately normal" as "data is normal" — they're different statements
  5. Forgetting sample size scaling — to halve the SE, need 4× more data
  6. Using normal approximation when np < 10 or n(1−p) < 10 for proportions — use exact binomial
  7. Confusing LLN with CLT — LLN says where the mean converges; CLT says HOW (in shape)
  8. Assuming finite variance — Cauchy and other heavy-tailed have ∞ variance; CLT fails
★ ON THE EXAM

"CLT statement?" → Sample mean of iid observations with finite variance is approximately Normal(μ, σ²/n) for large n.

"Standard error of the mean?" → σ / √n.

"When does CLT apply?" → Independent, identically distributed, finite variance; n ≥ 30 rule of thumb.

"Sample size to halve the margin of error?" → 4×.

"Sample size to 10× precision?" → 100×.

"CLT for sample proportion?" → p̂ ~ Normal(p, p(1−p)/n) when np ≥ 10 AND n(1−p) ≥ 10.

"σ unknown — use which distribution?" → t with n−1 degrees of freedom.

"Underlying data must be normal?" → No — that's the point of CLT.

"LLN vs CLT?" → LLN says x̄ → μ; CLT says (x̄ − μ)/(σ/√n) → Normal(0,1).

"Bootstrap?" → Resample with replacement to estimate sampling distribution; no normality assumed.

"CLT fails for which distributions?" → Those with infinite variance (e.g., Cauchy).

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Parameter (μ, σ, p) = population fact; statistic (x̄, s, p̂) = sample-based estimate
  • Sampling distribution = the distribution of a statistic across many possible samples
  • CLT: sample mean x̄ is approximately Normal(μ, σ²/n) for large n, regardless of underlying distribution
  • Standard error of the mean: SE = σ/√n (or s/√n when σ is unknown)
  • n ≥ 30 is a common rule of thumb; heavily skewed data may need much more
  • CLT requires: independent, identically distributed, finite variance, sufficient sample size
  • The data itself doesn't become normal — only the sample MEAN does
  • Sample proportion has its own CLT: p̂ ~ Normal(p, p(1−p)/n) when np ≥ 10 and n(1−p) ≥ 10
  • When σ is estimated from data (almost always), use t-distribution with df = n−1 instead of normal
  • Precision scales as 1/√n: 4× sample → 2× tighter; 100× sample → 10× tighter
  • LLN: x̄ converges to μ. CLT: x̄ fluctuates normally around μ.
  • Bootstrap (resampling with replacement) extends CLT-style inference to statistics where CLT doesn't directly apply
  • CLT is the foundation of confidence intervals (ch4) and most hypothesis tests (ch5)

Sample-size arithmetic: SE = σ/√n, so DOUBLING n divides the standard error by √2 (≈1.41) — to halve SE you must QUADRUPLE the sample.

📊 FIGURE — The Central Limit Theorem in action
The population (left) is badly skewed — but take samples of size n and plot their MEANS: that distribution (right) is approximately normal, centered at μ, with the smaller spread σ/√n. This is why z- and t-methods work even for non-normal data.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A confidence interval (CI) is the most useful single output in applied statistics — it gives you an estimate plus an honest range of uncertainty. Every survey poll, A/B test, scientific paper, and analytics report uses CIs. The DataCamp Data Scientist Associate exam tests building them, interpreting them, and choosing z vs t correctly. Most beginners get the interpretation subtly wrong — we'll fix that here.

The idea — point estimate plus uncertainty

CONFIDENCE INTERVAL FOR A MEAN

CI = x̄ ± (critical value) × SE

  x̄ = point estimate (sample mean)
  SE = standard error (σ/√n if σ known; s/√n otherwise)
  critical value = from normal or t-distribution, depending on conditions

The total (critical value × SE) piece is the margin of error (MOE). 
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# Sample of customer satisfaction scores
scores = np.array([7, 8, 6, 9, 8, 7, 8, 9, 6, 8, 7, 9, 8, 7, 8])
n = len(scores)
x_bar = scores.mean() # 7.67
s = scores.std(ddof=1) # 0.976 — sample SD (ddof=1!)
se = s / np.sqrt(n) # ≈ 0.252

# 95% CI using t-distribution (σ unknown — almost always the case)
df = n - 1
t_crit = stats.t.ppf(0.975, df=df) # ≈ 2.145
moe = t_crit * se # ≈ 0.540

ci_low = x_bar - moe # ≈ 7.13
ci_high = x_bar + moe # ≈ 8.20

# Interpretation: "We're 95% confident that the true mean satisfaction is between 7.13 and 8.20."

z-CI vs t-CI — which to use

CHOOSING THE CRITICAL VALUE
Use z (normal critical value) when:
  • Population σ is KNOWN
  • Or n is very large (n ≥ 30 is the rule of thumb; matters less these days)

Use t (Student's t critical value) when:
  • Population σ is UNKNOWN (almost always)
  • Population is approximately normal OR n is at least ~30 (CLT)

Modern practice: just use t. For large n it's nearly identical to z anyway, and it's correct when n is small. 
from scipy import stats

# Critical values for 95% CI
stats.norm.ppf(0.975) # 1.960 — z critical value (σ known case)
stats.t.ppf(0.975, df=10) # 2.228 — wider CI with small n
stats.t.ppf(0.975, df=30) # 2.042
stats.t.ppf(0.975, df=100) # 1.984 — very close to 1.96
stats.t.ppf(0.975, df=1000) # 1.962 — nearly z

# As n grows, t → z. With n ≥ 30 the difference is negligible.

z-CI form (σ known — rare in practice)

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# Example: from manufacturing, σ is known to be exactly 5 mm from calibration data
n = 50
x_bar = 100.2
sigma = 5

z_crit = stats.norm.ppf(0.975) # 1.96
se = sigma / np.sqrt(n) # ≈ 0.707
moe = z_crit * se # ≈ 1.386

ci = (x_bar - moe, x_bar + moe) # (98.81, 101.59)

t-CI form (σ unknown — almost always)

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# Real-world version — only have sample data
data = np.array([2.1, 3.4, 2.8, 4.1, 3.0, 3.9, 2.5, 3.2, 3.8, 2.7])
n = len(data)
x_bar = data.mean() # 3.15
s = data.std(ddof=1) # 0.683
se = s / np.sqrt(n) # 0.216

# 95% t-CI with df = n - 1
df = n - 1 # 9
t_crit = stats.t.ppf(0.975, df=df) # 2.262
moe = t_crit * se # 0.489

ci = (x_bar - moe, x_bar + moe)
# (2.66, 3.64)

# Or in one shot using scipy
ci_scipy = stats.t.interval(0.95, df=df, loc=x_bar, scale=se)
# Same answer

# Or with pandas
import pandas as pd
df_data = pd.Series(data)
ci_scipy = stats.t.interval(0.95, df=len(df_data)-1, loc=df_data.mean(), scale=df_data.sem())

Confidence level — choosing the % level

Confidenceαz critical (large n)
90%0.101.645
95%0.051.960 (most common)
99%0.012.576
99.9%0.0013.291

Higher confidence = wider interval. There's no free lunch — to be more sure your interval covers the true parameter, you accept a less-precise answer.

Interpretation — the most-misunderstood part

★ WHAT A 95% CI ACTUALLY MEANS

The correct frequentist interpretation:

"If we repeated the sampling process many times, building a 95% CI each time, about 95% of those intervals would contain the true parameter μ."

The CI you computed either does or doesn't contain μ — you just don't know which.

WRONG interpretations:

  • "There's a 95% probability that μ is in this specific interval." (μ is fixed; doesn't have a probability)
  • "95% of the data falls in this range." (That's about data, not μ)
  • "There's a 95% chance the experiment will produce a similar mean." (No)

Width of the CI — controlling precision

MOE FORMULA — what controls the width

MOE = z × σ / √n    (or t × s / √n)

Wider CI from:
  • Higher confidence (bigger z/t)
  • More variability (bigger σ or s)
  • Smaller sample size (smaller n in denominator)

Narrower CI from the opposites. 
# Sample size to achieve a target MOE
import math
sigma = 50
target_moe = 5
z = 1.96 # 95%

n_required = (z * sigma / target_moe) ** 2
n_required # ≈ 384.16
n_rounded = math.ceil(n_required) # 385

# 4× the sample → 2× narrower CI (precision scales as 1/√n)
# 100× sample → 10× narrower CI
# Always round UP for sample size to be safe

Reporting CIs

# Always report:
# • Point estimate (sample mean)
# • Confidence level (90%, 95%, etc.)
# • Bounds of the interval

# Style 1: "Mean satisfaction = 7.67 (95% CI: 7.13 to 8.20)"
# Style 2: "7.67 ± 0.54 (95% CI)"
# Style 3: "Mean = 7.67, 95% CI [7.13, 8.20]"

# AVOID reporting just the point estimate without uncertainty.
# Three things ruin reports:
# 1. No confidence interval (or other uncertainty measure)
# 2. CI without the level (95%? 90%?)
# 3. CI but no point estimate

Worked example — full A/B test analysis

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A/B test mean revenue

Scenario: Group A (control) vs Group B (new design). You measure revenue per visitor.

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# Sample data
np.random.seed(42)
a = np.random.exponential(scale=5, size=100) # mean ≈ 5
b = np.random.exponential(scale=5.5, size=100) # mean ≈ 5.5

# CI for group A
def mean_ci(data, level=0.95):
 n = len(data)
 x_bar = data.mean()
 s = data.std(ddof=1)
 se = s / np.sqrt(n)
 return stats.t.interval(level, df=n-1, loc=x_bar, scale=se)

ci_a = mean_ci(a) # e.g., (4.32, 5.78)
ci_b = mean_ci(b) # e.g., (4.87, 6.41)

# Mean revenue is higher in B, but the CIs OVERLAP — not definitively better
# For a more rigorous test, use difference-of-means CI or t-test (ch5)

# CI on the DIFFERENCE (more informative than overlapping CIs)
diff = b.mean() - a.mean()
se_diff = np.sqrt(a.var(ddof=1)/len(a) + b.var(ddof=1)/len(b))
df_diff = len(a) + len(b) - 2 # simplified — Welch's gives more accurate df
t_crit = stats.t.ppf(0.975, df=df_diff)
moe = t_crit * se_diff
ci_diff = (diff - moe, diff + moe)
# If 0 is INSIDE this CI → no significant difference detected
# If 0 is OUTSIDE → there's a statistically significant difference

Bootstrap CIs — when assumptions don't hold

import numpy as np

# Useful when:
# • Data is very skewed and n is small (CLT not yet kicked in)
# • You want a CI for a statistic other than the mean (median, ratio, etc.)
# • You need a CI without making distributional assumptions

data = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 100]) # tiny n, big outlier

n_boot = 10000
boot_means = []
for _ in range(n_boot):
 sample = np.random.choice(data, size=len(data), replace=True)
 boot_means.append(sample.mean())

ci_boot = np.percentile(boot_means, [2.5, 97.5])
# Empirical 95% CI from the resampling distribution

# Compare to t-CI on this data — they'll differ because data is very skewed
from scipy import stats
n = len(data)
ci_t = stats.t.interval(0.95, df=n-1, loc=data.mean(), scale=data.std(ddof=1)/np.sqrt(n))

# Bootstrap CI is usually more reliable for non-normal data with small n.

Common CI mistakes

⚠ TOP CI ERRORS
  1. "95% probability the parameter is in this CI" — most common misinterpretation
  2. Comparing two CIs for overlap as a significance test — sometimes works, sometimes doesn't; compute CI of the difference instead
  3. Using z when σ is unknown — use t, especially for smaller samples
  4. Using ddof=0 for sample SD — NumPy default underestimates; use ddof=1
  5. Forgetting CLT conditions — CI assumes the sampling distribution of the mean is approximately normal
  6. Not reporting confidence level — "the CI was (3, 7)" doesn't say if it's 90% or 99%
  7. Computing CI on heavily skewed small samples — better to bootstrap or transform first
  8. Using sample SD when computing margin from σ-known formula — mix-and-match formulas
  9. Reporting CI without the point estimate — readers need both
★ ON THE EXAM

"CI formula?" → point estimate ± critical value × SE.

"SE of the mean?" → s / √n (or σ / √n if known).

"When to use t instead of z?" → σ unknown (almost always); df = n − 1.

"95% CI critical z?" → 1.96.

"90% CI critical z?" → 1.645.

"99% CI critical z?" → 2.576.

"Halve the margin of error?" → 4× the sample size.

"Wider CI from?" → Higher confidence, more variability, smaller sample.

"Correct CI interpretation?" → "If we repeat sampling, ~95% of such intervals would contain μ" (NOT "95% probability μ is in this one").

"scipy 95% t-CI?" → stats.t.interval(0.95, df=n-1, loc=mean, scale=sem).

"Bootstrap CI?" → Resample with replacement, take percentiles of the resampled statistic.

"Two CIs overlap — significant?" → Not necessarily; check CI of the difference instead.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Confidence interval = point estimate ± margin of error
  • For a mean: x̄ ± (critical value × SE)
  • SE = s/√n (with ddof=1) or σ/√n if σ is known
  • Use t-distribution with df = n−1 when σ is unknown (the usual case)
  • Use z-distribution only when σ is known exactly (rare in practice)
  • z critical for 95% = 1.96; for 90% = 1.645; for 99% = 2.576
  • t critical values are larger than z for small n; converge to z as n → ∞
  • Correct interpretation: "If we repeat sampling, ~95% of CIs would contain the true μ"
  • WRONG: "There's a 95% probability that μ is in this specific CI"
  • To halve the margin of error, quadruple the sample size (precision ~ 1/√n)
  • Higher confidence = wider CI; lower confidence = narrower
  • Bootstrap CI works for any statistic and doesn't assume normality — useful for small n or skewed data
  • For comparing two groups, build a CI for the DIFFERENCE, not just check overlap
  • Use scipy.stats.t.interval(0.95, df, loc, scale) for one-line CI computation
📊 FIGURE — What "95% confidence" actually means
Each horizontal bar is the interval from one sample. The parameter μ (dashed) never moves — the INTERVALS vary. In the long run about 95% of them capture μ; the red one missed. A single computed interval either contains μ or not — the 95% describes the procedure.
