◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Proportions are everywhere — conversion rates, click-through rates, defect rates, poll results, churn percentages. CIs for proportions answer "what's the true rate, plus or minus?". The DataCamp Data Scientist Associate exam tests Wald and Wilson intervals, the np ≥ 10 condition, and sample size planning for surveys and A/B tests.

Setup — Bernoulli trials, sample proportion

SAMPLE PROPORTION
Take n independent Bernoulli(p) trials.
p̂ = (number of successes) / n — the sample proportion.

By CLT (when conditions hold): p̂ ~ Normal(p, p(1−p)/n)

SE(p̂) = √[p(1−p)/n] when p is known
SE(p̂) ≈ √[p̂(1−p̂)/n] in practice (plug in p̂) 
import numpy as np

# 1000 site visitors, 47 converted
n = 1000
x = 47
p_hat = x / n # 0.047

# Sample SE estimated from p_hat
se = np.sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n) # ≈ 0.00669

# This is the foundation for proportion CIs.

The Wald (normal-approximation) CI — the textbook formula

WALD CI

p̂ ± z × √[p̂(1−p̂)/n]

Simple, intuitive — but has bad coverage when p is near 0 or 1, or when n is small.

Use only when np̂ ≥ 10 AND n(1−p̂) ≥ 10 (the success/failure condition). 
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# Wald CI by hand
n = 1000
p_hat = 47 / n # 0.047
se = np.sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n)
z = stats.norm.ppf(0.975) # 1.96

moe = z * se
ci_wald = (p_hat - moe, p_hat + moe)
# ≈ (0.0339, 0.0601)

# Check conditions
n * p_hat # 47 ≥ 10 ✓
n * (1 - p_hat) # 953 ≥ 10 ✓
# Both clear → Wald CI is reasonable

# Quick scipy version
ci_scipy = stats.norm.interval(0.95, loc=p_hat, scale=se)
⚠ WALD FAILS WHEN p IS NEAR 0 OR 1

If p̂ = 0 or p̂ = 1, Wald gives a CI of zero width — clearly wrong.

If counts are small (say x = 2 out of 50), Wald undercovers — the actual 95% CI captures the true p less than 95% of the time.

For these cases, use Wilson or Agresti-Coull intervals.

The Wilson score CI — better in nearly every case

WILSON SCORE CI
More accurate than Wald, especially for small samples or extreme p̂. The default in modern stats packages.

center = (p̂ + z²/(2n)) / (1 + z²/n)
half-width = z × √[(p̂(1−p̂) + z²/(4n)) / n] / (1 + z²/n)

Looks ugly but works much better than Wald. Always available via libraries. 
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_confint

# Wilson CI (recommended)
ci = proportion_confint(count=47, nobs=1000, alpha=0.05, method='wilson')
# Returns (lower, upper) e.g., (0.0356, 0.0621)

# Default method='normal' is Wald — usually want to explicitly pick wilson
# Alternative methods:
proportion_confint(47, 1000, alpha=0.05, method='wilson')
proportion_confint(47, 1000, alpha=0.05, method='agresti_coull') # also good
proportion_confint(47, 1000, alpha=0.05, method='beta') # exact (Clopper-Pearson)

# Wilson handles edge cases (p̂ near 0 or 1) gracefully without breaking

The Agresti-Coull CI — Wilson's simpler cousin

AGRESTI-COULL CI
Practically as accurate as Wilson but easier to compute by hand.

Step 1: pretend you have 2 extra successes and 2 extra failures.
  ñ = n + 4    p̃ = (x + 2) / (n + 4)

Step 2: apply Wald to the adjusted values.
  p̃ ± z × √[p̃(1−p̃)/ñ] 
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# By hand
n, x = 1000, 47
n_adj = n + 4
p_adj = (x + 2) / n_adj # ≈ 0.0488
se_adj = np.sqrt(p_adj * (1 - p_adj) / n_adj)
z = stats.norm.ppf(0.975)

ci_ac = (p_adj - z*se_adj, p_adj + z*se_adj)
# Close to Wilson, much better than Wald for extreme p

The exact (Clopper-Pearson) CI

from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_confint

# Uses the binomial CDF directly — always covers at least 95%
# Conservative (slightly wider than needed) but never undercovers
ci_exact = proportion_confint(47, 1000, alpha=0.05, method='beta')

# When to use:
# - Small samples
# - Regulatory or medical contexts where false confidence is unacceptable
# - When p̂ is exactly 0 or 1 (other methods may fail)

Comparing the four methods

MethodWhen to usePros / Cons
Wald (normal)Large n, p̂ near 0.5Simple; bad for extreme p̂ or small n
WilsonAlmost any caseBest general purpose
Agresti-CoullHand calculationsAlmost as accurate as Wilson, simpler formula
Clopper-PearsonTiny n; regulatoryAlways covers but conservative (wider than needed)
★ PRACTICAL RULE

Default to Wilson. Only use Wald if a textbook or exam question specifically asks for "the normal approximation" CI for proportions.

The success/failure condition

CONDITION FOR NORMAL APPROXIMATION
np̂ ≥ 10  AND  n(1 − p̂) ≥ 10

Some sources use 5 or 15 — DataCamp uses 10.
In words: need at least 10 successes AND 10 failures.
When either count is small, switch to Wilson or exact methods. 
# Examples
# n=1000, p̂=0.047 → 47 successes, 953 failures → ✓ both ≥ 10, normal OK
# n=50, p̂=0.05 → 2.5 successes, 47.5 failures → ✗ fails, use Wilson
# n=20, p̂=0.5 → 10 successes, 10 failures → ✓ borderline OK
# n=100, p̂=0.99 → 99 successes, 1 failure → ✗ use Wilson or exact

Sample size planning for proportions

SAMPLE SIZE FOR DESIRED MARGIN OF ERROR
Starting from MOE = z × √[p(1−p)/n], solve for n:

n = (z / MOE)² × p(1−p)

If p is unknown, use the worst case p = 0.5 (maximum of p(1−p)). 
import math

# Survey question: "What % approve of policy X?"
# Want 95% CI with MOE = ±3 percentage points

z = 1.96
moe = 0.03

# Without prior knowledge of p, use p = 0.5 (worst case)
n_worst = (z / moe) ** 2 * 0.5 * 0.5
math.ceil(n_worst) # 1068 — classic political poll size

# If you have a prior estimate, e.g., p ≈ 0.20:
n_prior = (z / moe) ** 2 * 0.20 * 0.80
math.ceil(n_prior) # 683 — smaller sample needed

# Higher precision: MOE = ±1 pp → n_worst ≈ 9604
# Lower confidence: 90% CI (z=1.645) → smaller n
# Larger expected variability (p near 0.5) → bigger n

Worked example — A/B test with proportions

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Comparing two conversion rates

Scenario: Variant A: 4,800 visitors, 240 conversions (5.0%). Variant B: 4,950 visitors, 297 conversions (6.0%). Is the difference statistically meaningful?

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_confint, confint_proportions_2indep

# Individual CIs
ci_a = proportion_confint(240, 4800, alpha=0.05, method='wilson')
ci_b = proportion_confint(297, 4950, alpha=0.05, method='wilson')
# ci_a ≈ (0.0441, 0.0566) — about 4.4% to 5.7%
# ci_b ≈ (0.0536, 0.0670) — about 5.4% to 6.7%
# CIs overlap slightly — don't conclude from this!

# CI for the DIFFERENCE (proper test)
p_a = 240/4800
p_b = 297/4950
diff = p_b - p_a # 0.010
se_diff = np.sqrt(p_a*(1-p_a)/4800 + p_b*(1-p_b)/4950)
z = 1.96
ci_diff = (diff - z*se_diff, diff + z*se_diff)
# ≈ (0.0014, 0.0186)
# 0 is NOT in the CI → there IS a significant difference
# B is better by between 0.14 and 1.86 percentage points

# Use statsmodels for proper 2-proportion CI
ci_diff_sm = confint_proportions_2indep(
 count1=297, nobs1=4950,
 count2=240, nobs2=4800,
 alpha=0.05, method='wald'
)

Why "comparing two CIs for overlap" can be misleading

⚠ THE CI-OVERLAP TRAP

It's common to look at two CIs and say "they overlap → no difference; they don't overlap → significant difference."

The first part is unreliable. Two CIs can OVERLAP and yet the difference is statistically significant (e.g., A: 5.0±1.0, B: 6.5±1.0 — overlap of 0.5 but difference is solid).

Always compute the CI of the DIFFERENCE (or run a two-sample test) to be sure.

The "non-overlapping → significant" half IS reliable.

Real-world considerations

Finite population correction

# If your sample is more than 5% of the population, the SE is overestimated
# Apply finite population correction:
# SE_adjusted = SE * sqrt((N - n) / (N - 1))
# where N is the population size

# For most A/B tests and surveys this doesn't matter (sample << population)
# Comes up in audit work, quality control, internal HR studies

Cluster sampling violates independence

# If you sample by HOUSEHOLD then interview multiple people per household,
# the independence assumption fails (members are correlated)
# Effective sample size is smaller than n; CIs that pretend otherwise are too narrow
# Use cluster-aware methods (survey package in R, statsmodels.regression.linear_model.OLS with cluster SEs in Python)

Worked example — small-sample medical study

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Why Wilson, not Wald

Scenario: A pilot study tests a new drug. Out of 25 patients, 3 experienced a rare side effect.

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_confint

n, x = 25, 3
p_hat = x / n # 0.12

# Conditions check:
n * p_hat # 3 — FAILS the n*p ≥ 10 rule
# Wald CI here is unreliable

# Wald (DON'T USE — for comparison)
se = np.sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n)
ci_wald = (p_hat - 1.96*se, p_hat + 1.96*se)
# ≈ (-0.007, 0.247) — LOWER BOUND NEGATIVE (impossible!)

# Wilson
ci_wilson = proportion_confint(x, n, alpha=0.05, method='wilson')
# ≈ (0.042, 0.300) — sensible bounds

# Exact (Clopper-Pearson)
ci_exact = proportion_confint(x, n, alpha=0.05, method='beta')
# ≈ (0.025, 0.312) — slightly wider, conservative

# Always prefer Wilson or exact for small n or extreme p̂

Common mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Using Wald CI when np < 10 or n(1−p) < 10 — Wilson is the safe default
  2. Wald CI dipping below 0 or above 1 — math says yes, reality says no; switch methods
  3. Comparing two proportion CIs for overlap as a significance test — unreliable; compute CI of difference
  4. Using sample p̂ for sample-size planning when conservative thing is to use p = 0.5
  5. Treating clustered/dependent data as independent — same person sampled twice, household effects
  6. Ignoring finite population correction in audit-style sampling (rarely matters in A/B tests)
  7. Confusing the SE of p̂ with the SD of the data — proportions aren't a "data SD"; their SD comes from p(1−p)/n
  8. Reporting p̂ without CI — point estimate alone is misleading
★ ON THE EXAM

"CI for proportion (Wald)?" → p̂ ± z × √[p̂(1−p̂)/n].

"SE of proportion?" → √[p̂(1−p̂)/n].

"Success/failure condition?" → np̂ ≥ 10 AND n(1−p̂) ≥ 10.

"Best general method for proportion CI?" → Wilson score.

"Method for small n or extreme p̂?" → Wilson or Clopper-Pearson (exact).

"Worst-case sample size?" → Use p = 0.5 → n = (z/MOE)² × 0.25.

"Survey with MOE = ±3 pp, 95% CI?" → n ≈ 1068.

"Wald gives a negative lower bound?" → Switch to Wilson or exact.

"Two CIs barely overlap — significant difference?" → Maybe; compute CI of the difference.

"Two CIs don't overlap — significant?" → Yes, the difference is significant.

"statsmodels proportion CI?" → proportion_confint(x, n, alpha, method='wilson').

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Sample proportion p̂ = successes / n; estimates the true rate p
  • Wald CI: p̂ ± z × √[p̂(1−p̂)/n] — simple but bad for small n or extreme p
  • Wilson score CI is more accurate and the recommended default
  • Agresti-Coull adds 2 successes and 2 failures, then applies Wald — close to Wilson
  • Clopper-Pearson uses the exact binomial — conservative but never undercovers
  • Success/failure condition: need np̂ ≥ 10 AND n(1−p̂) ≥ 10 for Wald to be reasonable
  • Wald can produce CIs that go below 0 or above 1 — Wilson does not
  • Sample size for ±MOE at 95% confidence: n = (1.96 / MOE)² × p(1−p)
  • Worst-case planning uses p = 0.5, giving the maximum sample size
  • To compare two proportions, compute the CI of the difference (or do a two-proportion test)
  • Comparing CI overlap is unreliable for significance — non-overlap implies significant, overlap doesn't preclude it
  • statsmodels.stats.proportion.proportion_confint handles all the methods with one call
  • Cluster/dependent data violates the independence assumption — adjust if relevant
📊 FIGURE — What "95% confidence" actually means
Each horizontal bar is the interval from one sample. The parameter μ (dashed) never moves — the INTERVALS vary. In the long run about 95% of them capture μ; the red one missed. A single computed interval either contains μ or not — the 95% describes the procedure.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

"How big a sample do I need?" is the most-asked question in applied stats — and getting it wrong wastes time, money, and trust. Too small a sample yields inconclusive answers; too large wastes resources. Sample-size planning shows up in surveys, A/B tests, clinical trials, quality audits, and the DataCamp Data Scientist Associate exam tests both means and proportions.

The general principle

PRECISION-DRIVEN SAMPLE SIZE
Start with the margin-of-error formula and solve for n.

For a mean:   n = (z × σ / MOE)²
For a proportion:   n = (z / MOE)² × p(1−p)

Inputs you must decide:
  • Confidence level (95%, 99%) → critical value z
  • Desired margin of error (MOE)
  • Variability estimate (σ for means, p for proportions)

Sample size for a mean

import math
from scipy import stats

# Want to estimate average customer LTV within ±$5 at 95% confidence
# Past data suggests σ ≈ $50

z = stats.norm.ppf(0.975) # 1.96
sigma = 50
moe = 5

n = (z * sigma / moe) ** 2 # 384.16
n_required = math.ceil(n) # 385 — always round UP

# Tighter MOE? Bigger n.
# Different MOEs:
# MOE = $10 → n = 97
# MOE = $5 → n = 385
# MOE = $2 → n = 2401
# MOE = $1 → n = 9604
# Precision scales as 1/√n — halving MOE needs 4× the sample

Where σ comes from when you don't know it

  • Pilot study: collect ~30 observations, compute s, use that
  • Prior research / industry benchmarks: published values
  • Range / 4 rule: for roughly normal data, σ ≈ (max − min) / 4
  • Conservative upper bound: if uncertain, use a larger σ and accept a bigger n

Sample size for a proportion

import math
from scipy import stats

# Survey question: "What % support policy X?"
# Want 95% CI with MOE = ±3 percentage points

z = stats.norm.ppf(0.975) # 1.96
moe = 0.03

# With a prior estimate p ≈ 0.20
p_prior = 0.20
n_prior = (z / moe) ** 2 * p_prior * (1 - p_prior)
math.ceil(n_prior) # 683

# Worst-case (no prior info — use p = 0.5)
p_worst = 0.5
n_worst = (z / moe) ** 2 * p_worst * (1 - p_worst)
math.ceil(n_worst) # 1068 — classic political poll size

# Common targets:
# MOE = ±5 pp at 95% → n ≈ 385
# MOE = ±3 pp at 95% → n ≈ 1068
# MOE = ±2 pp at 95% → n ≈ 2401
# MOE = ±1 pp at 95% → n ≈ 9604

Why p(1−p) is maximized at p = 0.5

# p(1−p) at various p:
# p = 0.1 → 0.09
# p = 0.3 → 0.21
# p = 0.5 → 0.25 ← maximum
# p = 0.7 → 0.21
# p = 0.9 → 0.09

# If you have no prior knowledge, p = 0.5 gives the LARGEST n needed
# → safe upper bound for planning
# Knowing p is far from 0.5 lets you save sample size dramatically

Power analysis — sample size for hypothesis tests

SAMPLE SIZE FOR A TWO-SAMPLE TEST
Different from "precision-driven" CIs — for detecting a true effect:

n per group ≈ ((zα/2 + zβ) × σ / Δ)² × 2

Inputs:
  • α: significance level (typically 0.05 → zα/2 = 1.96)
  • β: false-negative rate (typically 0.20 → power = 1 − β = 0.80, zβ = 0.84)
  • σ: standard deviation of the outcome
  • Δ: minimum detectable effect size you care about 
import math
from scipy import stats

# A/B test: detect a $2 difference in mean revenue, with σ = $10
# α = 0.05 (two-sided), power = 0.80

z_alpha = stats.norm.ppf(0.975) # 1.96 — two-sided
z_beta = stats.norm.ppf(0.80) # 0.842

sigma = 10
delta = 2

n_per_group = ((z_alpha + z_beta) * sigma / delta) ** 2 * 2
math.ceil(n_per_group) # 393 per group → 786 total

# Smaller effect to detect = MUCH bigger n
# Detect $1 instead of $2: 4× the sample size
# Higher power (0.90 vs 0.80): ~30% more sample

# Use statsmodels for the canonical version
from statsmodels.stats.power import TTestIndPower
analysis = TTestIndPower()
n_each = analysis.solve_power(effect_size=delta/sigma, alpha=0.05, power=0.80)
# returns ~394 per group

Sample size for a proportion difference

import math
from scipy import stats

# A/B test detecting baseline 5% conversion vs new 6% (1pp lift)
# α = 0.05 two-sided, power = 0.80

p1 = 0.05
p2 = 0.06
delta = p2 - p1 # 0.01

p_bar = (p1 + p2) / 2 # 0.055
z_alpha = 1.96
z_beta = 0.842

# Pooled variance for the null assumption
var_null = 2 * p_bar * (1 - p_bar)
# Alternative variance
var_alt = p1*(1-p1) + p2*(1-p2)

n_per_group = ((z_alpha * math.sqrt(var_null) + z_beta * math.sqrt(var_alt)) / delta) ** 2
math.ceil(n_per_group) # ≈ 8378 per group → 16756 total

# Lesson: detecting small relative differences requires HUGE samples
# 5% → 6% (1pp) needs ~16k visitors
# 5% → 7% (2pp) needs ~4k
# 5% → 10% (5pp) needs ~700
# Use statsmodels for cleaner code:
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportions_chisquare, samplesize_proportions_2indep_onetail
# or run a power analysis via statsmodels.stats.power.NormalIndPower for a Z-approach

Trade-offs — the four levers

★ FOUR THINGS YOU CAN CHANGE
  • Sample size (n): bigger n = more power and narrower CIs
  • Effect size (Δ): only detecting bigger effects requires fewer samples
  • Significance level (α): stricter α (e.g., 0.01) needs more samples
  • Power (1 − β): higher power needs more samples

Fix any three → the fourth is determined.

One-sided vs two-sided

from scipy import stats

# Two-sided 95% CI uses z = 1.96 (probability 0.025 in each tail)
# One-sided 95% bound uses z = 1.645 (probability 0.05 in one tail)

z_two = stats.norm.ppf(0.975) # 1.96 (two-sided)
z_one = stats.norm.ppf(0.95) # 1.645 (one-sided)

# One-sided needs ~70% as many samples as two-sided for the same MOE
# Only justified when you genuinely only care about ONE direction
# e.g., upper bound on a defect rate; one-sided lower bound on a guarantee

Worked example — A/B test sample planning

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — How many users per variant?

Scenario: Your control converts at 4%. You want 80% power to detect a 0.5 percentage-point lift (4.0% → 4.5%) at α = 0.05.

import math
from statsmodels.stats.power import NormalIndPower
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_effectsize

p1 = 0.040
p2 = 0.045

# Convert to Cohen's h effect size (the standard scale for proportions)
effect_size = proportion_effectsize(p1, p2)

analysis = NormalIndPower()
n_per_group = analysis.solve_power(
 effect_size=abs(effect_size),
 alpha=0.05,
 power=0.80,
 alternative='two-sided'
)
math.ceil(n_per_group) # ≈ 53000 per group

# Conclusion: 53k per variant — ~106k total visitors needed
# If traffic is 1000/day, the test runs ~106 days
# If you must finish in 30 days, you can only detect bigger effects
# Often this is the moment you re-think the experiment

# Sensitivity analysis — what effects CAN you detect?
for delta in [0.005, 0.010, 0.020, 0.050]:
 p2_alt = p1 + delta
 es = abs(proportion_effectsize(p1, p2_alt))
 n = analysis.solve_power(effect_size=es, alpha=0.05, power=0.80)
 print(f"To detect +{delta*100:.1f}pp: n = {math.ceil(n)} per group")
# +0.5pp: 53k ← original
# +1.0pp: 13k
# +2.0pp: 3k
# +5.0pp: ~500

Adjusting for multiple comparisons

# If running multiple tests, your effective α inflates
# Bonferroni correction: use α/k for each of k tests
# For example, 10 tests at overall α = 0.05 → each test uses α = 0.005
# Stricter α → bigger required sample sizes per test

# Sample size for one comparison at α = 0.005:
z_alpha_corrected = stats.norm.ppf(1 - 0.005/2) # 2.807
# vs 1.96 for uncorrected
# n grows by factor (2.807/1.96)² ≈ 2.05 — roughly DOUBLE
# Major reason to limit number of A/B test variants

Practical sample-size guidelines

ScenarioTypical n
National political poll (95%, ±3pp)~1,000-1,500
Marketing A/B test (5% baseline, 1pp lift)10k-20k per variant
Customer satisfaction survey (±5%)~400
Quality control audit (1% defect rate, ±0.5pp)~1,500
Clinical trial (moderate effect)100-1000 per group
Pilot study (just to estimate σ)~30

Common sample-size planning mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Forgetting to round UP — round-down can undershoot the precision you need
  2. Using ddof=0 to estimate σ from a pilot — use ddof=1 for sample SD
  3. Optimistic effect-size assumptions — assuming a big effect produces small sample sizes; if actual effect is smaller, test is underpowered
  4. Forgetting that A/B tests need n PER GROUP — double for total visitors needed
  5. Mixing one-sided and two-sided assumptions — one-sided gives smaller n but only valid if direction is pre-specified
  6. Not adjusting for multiple comparisons — running 10 tests at α = 0.05 means 1 false positive expected even if all nulls true
  7. Treating clustered data as independent — same user counted multiple times inflates effective n
  8. Sample-size hacking — peeking at results mid-test and stopping when "significant" inflates false positives
★ ON THE EXAM

"Sample size for mean with given MOE?" → n = (z × σ / MOE)².

"Sample size for proportion with given MOE?" → n = (z / MOE)² × p(1−p).

"Halve MOE?" → 4× sample size.

"Worst-case for proportion sample size?" → p = 0.5 → maximum n.

"Why p = 0.5?" → Maximizes p(1−p) = 0.25.

"Power = 0.80 means?" → 80% chance of detecting a true effect (β = 0.20).

"Bonferroni correction?" → Divide α by k for k tests.

"Always round UP for n?" → Yes — rounding down undershoots the desired precision.

"One-sided vs two-sided sample size?" → One-sided is smaller (~70%), but only valid if direction is fixed in advance.

"Cohen's h?" → Standardized effect size for proportions.

"statsmodels for power analysis?" → TTestIndPower, NormalIndPower.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Sample size is driven by precision (CI width) or by detection (statistical power)
  • For a mean CI: n = (z × σ / MOE)²
  • For a proportion CI: n = (z / MOE)² × p(1−p); worst case at p = 0.5
  • Halving the margin of error needs 4× the sample size (precision ~ 1/√n)
  • Use a pilot study, prior data, or worst-case to estimate σ or p before planning
  • Always round n UP — never down
  • For A/B testing, sample-size planning uses both α and β (power); larger effect to detect = smaller n
  • Power analysis: typical defaults are α = 0.05 and power = 0.80
  • A/B tests for small lifts (1pp) on small baselines (5%) need huge samples (10k+ per variant)
  • Bonferroni-correcting α for k comparisons multiplies the per-test sample size by ~2 for k = 10
  • One-sided tests need fewer samples, but only if direction is decided in advance
  • Use statsmodels.stats.power for canonical power calculations in code
  • Sample-size planning is the single biggest determinant of experiment success — don't skip it

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Hypothesis testing is how we decide whether a pattern is real or random noise. Every A/B test, scientific finding, clinical trial, and "is this treatment effective" question reduces to a hypothesis test. The DataCamp Data Scientist Associate exam tests the framework, p-value interpretation, type I/II errors, and choosing between one-sided and two-sided tests. Most beginners get p-value interpretation wrong — we'll fix that.

The basic setup

TWO COMPETING HYPOTHESES
H₀ (null hypothesis): the boring/default assumption (no effect, no difference, status quo).
H₁ or Hₐ (alternative): the interesting claim you'd need evidence to support.

Hypothesis testing is structured like a court trial:
  • H₀ is "innocent until proven guilty"
  • You collect data (evidence)
  • You compute a p-value (strength of evidence)
  • If evidence is strong enough, REJECT H₀ — otherwise FAIL TO REJECT H₀ 
# Example: testing a coin for fairness
# H₀: p = 0.5 (coin is fair)
# H₁: p ≠ 0.5 (coin is biased)

# Example: testing if a new drug works
# H₀: μ_new = μ_placebo (no improvement)
# H₁: μ_new > μ_placebo (drug improves outcomes)

# Example: A/B test for conversion rate
# H₀: p_A = p_B (no difference between variants)
# H₁: p_A ≠ p_B (variants differ)

One-sided vs two-sided

Test typeH₁Use when
Two-sidedμ ≠ μ₀You care about ANY direction of difference (default)
One-sided (right)μ > μ₀You only care if it's bigger
One-sided (left)μ < μ₀You only care if it's smaller
⚠ DON'T PICK ONE-SIDED AFTER SEEING THE DATA

You must decide one-sided vs two-sided BEFORE collecting data — based on the question's logic, not on which direction the data went.

"My data shows B is higher, so I'll use a one-sided test to get a smaller p-value" is data dredging. Reviewers and auditors will reject it.

Default to two-sided unless one direction is genuinely irrelevant (e.g., a safety test where only WORSE outcomes matter).

The p-value — the central statistic

P-VALUE DEFINITION
Assuming H₀ is true, the probability of seeing data at least as extreme as what you observed.

Small p-value (e.g., < 0.05): the data would be unusual under H₀ → evidence against H₀.
Large p-value: data is consistent with H₀ → not enough evidence to reject. 
# Example: flip a coin 100 times, get 65 heads
# H₀: p = 0.5

from scipy import stats

# Under H₀, count of heads ~ Binomial(n=100, p=0.5)
# Mean = 50, SD = 5
# Observed count of heads = 65

# Two-sided p-value: P(|X - 50| ≥ 15) under H₀
# = P(X ≤ 35) + P(X ≥ 65)
p_one_side = stats.binom.sf(64, n=100, p=0.5) # P(X ≥ 65) ≈ 0.00176
p_two_sided = 2 * p_one_side # ≈ 0.00352

# Or use the built-in binomial test
result = stats.binomtest(k=65, n=100, p=0.5)
result.pvalue # 0.00352

# Tiny p-value — we'd see this result less than 1% of the time if coin were fair
# REJECT H₀ — coin is biased
⚠ WHAT P-VALUE IS NOT

Common WRONG interpretations:

  • "P(H₀ is true)" — wrong. P-values don't tell you the probability of any hypothesis.
  • "P(observed by chance)" — wrong. EVERY observation has some probability under H₀; the p-value is about extremity.
  • "1 − P(H₁ is true)" — wrong. Says nothing about how likely H₁ is.
  • "P(replicating the result)" — wrong. The p-value of a replication depends on its sample size.

The right framing: "If the null were true, would I see data this extreme as often as I did?"

The significance level α

SIGNIFICANCE LEVEL α
Your pre-chosen threshold for "small enough" p-value.

Common choices: 0.05 (most common), 0.01 (strict), 0.10 (lenient).
Reject H₀ when p < α; fail to reject when p ≥ α.

α is the maximum probability you're willing to wrongly reject a true H₀ (false positive rate). 
# Example: α = 0.05
# Coin test p-value = 0.00352 — much less than 0.05 → reject H₀, coin is biased
# Different example: p-value = 0.08 → fail to reject (at α = 0.05)

# Note: "fail to reject" is NOT "accept H₀" — important distinction!
# It just means "I don't have enough evidence to overturn H₀"
# H₀ might still be false; you just didn't catch it

Type I and Type II errors

Reality: H₀ TRUEReality: H₀ FALSE
Decision: Reject H₀Type I error (α)
False positive		Correct decision
(Power = 1−β)
Decision: Fail to rejectCorrect decisionType II error (β)
False negative
★ MEMORIZE THE TRADEOFF
  • α = P(reject H₀ | H₀ true) = Type I error rate — false positive
  • β = P(fail to reject H₀ | H₀ false) = Type II error rate — false negative
  • Power = 1 − β = probability of correctly detecting a real effect

Lowering α (stricter test) increases β (more false negatives). Lowering both at once requires more data.

# Real-world analogies
# Type I (false positive): convicting an innocent person
# Type II (false negative): letting a guilty person go free
# α = 0.05 means: 5% of innocent people get wrongly convicted if 
# the test is repeated under the null

# Medical screening:
# Type I: telling a healthy patient they have cancer (psychological harm, retesting)
# Type II: missing a patient who actually has cancer (more serious typically)
# → Medical screens often accept high α to keep β low

The general hypothesis test procedure

★ FIVE STEPS FOR EVERY TEST
  1. State H₀ and H₁ in terms of the population parameter you care about
  2. Choose α (and decide one-sided vs two-sided) BEFORE seeing data
  3. Compute the test statistic (z, t, chi-square, etc.) from your sample
  4. Find the p-value from the appropriate distribution
  5. Decision: reject H₀ if p < α — and report a sensible conclusion in plain English

Step 3 — the test statistic in general

TEST STATISTIC FORMULA (Z OR T)

test statistic = (observed − null value) / SE

How many standard errors is the observation from the null hypothesis value?
If it's far from 0 (more than ~2), the data is inconsistent with H₀. 
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# Example: test whether mean is different from 100
sample = np.array([102, 98, 105, 99, 103, 100, 101, 104, 97, 102])

n = len(sample)
x_bar = sample.mean() # 101.1
s = sample.std(ddof=1) # 2.51
se = s / np.sqrt(n) # 0.794
null_value = 100

# t-statistic
t_stat = (x_bar - null_value) / se # 1.385

# Two-sided p-value
df = n - 1
p_value = 2 * (1 - stats.t.cdf(abs(t_stat), df=df))
# = 0.199

# Or directly with scipy
result = stats.ttest_1samp(sample, popmean=100)
result.statistic # 1.385
result.pvalue # 0.199

# p = 0.199 > 0.05 → fail to reject H₀ at α = 0.05
# We don't have enough evidence that the mean differs from 100

p-value vs confidence interval — they agree

★ DUALITY

A two-sided test at α = 0.05 rejects H₀: μ = μ₀ if and only if the 95% CI does NOT contain μ₀.

Equivalent ways to ask the same question:

  • "Is the p-value < 0.05?"
  • "Is μ₀ outside the 95% CI?"

Two-sided 95% test ↔ 95% CI. One-sided 95% test ↔ 90% CI. The duality lets you cross-check.

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# Same sample as before
sample = np.array([102, 98, 105, 99, 103, 100, 101, 104, 97, 102])
n = len(sample)

# 95% CI
ci = stats.t.interval(0.95, df=n-1, loc=sample.mean(),
 scale=sample.std(ddof=1)/np.sqrt(n))
# (99.30, 102.90) — CI contains 100

# Test at α = 0.05
result = stats.ttest_1samp(sample, popmean=100)
result.pvalue # 0.199 > 0.05 → fail to reject

# Consistent: 100 is in the CI, and we fail to reject H₀: μ = 100
# Try H₀: μ = 95 instead?
# 95 is NOT in the CI → we'd reject H₀: μ = 95

Statistical vs practical significance

⚠ "SIGNIFICANT" ≠ "IMPORTANT"

With enough data, you can detect any nonzero difference as "statistically significant" — even one too small to matter.

Example: with n = 10 million, a 0.001 percentage-point lift in conversion rate is significant (p < 0.001), but probably doesn't justify any business decision.

Always report:

  • The p-value (statistical significance)
  • The effect size or CI (magnitude)
  • The practical interpretation (is this difference big enough to matter?)

Multiple comparisons — the family-wise error problem

# Running 20 tests at α = 0.05, ALL nulls true:
# Expected false positives = 20 × 0.05 = 1
# At least one false positive: probability ≈ 1 - 0.95²⁰ ≈ 0.64
# More than half the time, you'd see a "significant" result from PURE chance.

# Solutions:
# Bonferroni — use α/k per test
# False Discovery Rate (FDR) — control proportion of false discoveries

# Bonferroni example: 10 tests at overall α = 0.05 → each at α = 0.005
from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests
p_values = [0.01, 0.03, 0.04, 0.06, 0.001, 0.5, 0.02, 0.07, 0.001, 0.4]
reject, p_corrected, _, _ = multipletests(p_values, alpha=0.05, method='bonferroni')
# Compare to original — fewer significant after correction

# FDR (Benjamini-Hochberg) — less strict
reject, p_corrected, _, _ = multipletests(p_values, alpha=0.05, method='fdr_bh')

Worked example — A/B test framework

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — End-to-end test

Scenario: You run an A/B test on a checkout flow.
Control: 5000 users, 250 conversions (5.0%)
Variant: 5000 users, 300 conversions (6.0%)
Is the variant better?

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportions_ztest

# Step 1: state hypotheses
# H₀: p_variant = p_control
# H₁: p_variant ≠ p_control (two-sided — could go either way)

# Step 2: choose α = 0.05 (typical) BEFORE the test
alpha = 0.05

# Step 3: compute test statistic
count = np.array([250, 300]) # successes per group
nobs = np.array([5000, 5000]) # total per group
z_stat, p_value = proportions_ztest(count, nobs)
# z_stat ≈ -2.28
# p_value ≈ 0.0226

# Step 4: decision
if p_value < alpha:
 print("Reject H₀ — variant significantly different")
else:
 print("Fail to reject H₀")
# → Reject H₀: variant differs from control

# Step 5: ALSO report effect size and CI
p_c = 250/5000
p_v = 300/5000
diff = p_v - p_c # 0.01 — 1 percentage point lift
# Approximate 95% CI for the difference
se_diff = np.sqrt(p_c*(1-p_c)/5000 + p_v*(1-p_v)/5000)
ci = (diff - 1.96*se_diff, diff + 1.96*se_diff)
# ≈ (0.0015, 0.0185)

# Conclusion in plain English:
# "Variant lifts conversion from 5.0% to 6.0% — a 1pp absolute increase
# (95% CI 0.15 to 1.85 pp), p = 0.023. The improvement is real
# but modest; verify ROI before rollout."

Common hypothesis-testing mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Choosing one-sided after seeing the data — data dredging; invalid
  2. Misinterpreting p as "probability null is true" — wrong by construction
  3. Treating "fail to reject" as "accept H₀" — different things; absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence
  4. P-hacking — running many tests, reporting only the significant ones — inflates false positive rate
  5. Confusing statistical and practical significance — huge n makes tiny effects "significant"
  6. Stopping the test as soon as it crosses p < 0.05 — inflates Type I error rate
  7. Not reporting effect size or CI — p-value alone is insufficient
  8. Forgetting multiple-comparison correction when running many tests
  9. Comparing two CIs for overlap as a significance test — unreliable; compute CI of the difference
  10. Power = α confusion — power = 1 − β, not related to α directly
★ ON THE EXAM

"H₀ vs H₁?" → null (boring default) vs alternative (interesting claim).

"P-value definition?" → P(data this extreme or more | H₀ true).

"Reject H₀ when?" → p < α.

"Type I error?" → reject H₀ when it's actually true; rate = α.

"Type II error?" → fail to reject H₀ when it's actually false; rate = β.

"Power?" → 1 − β; probability of correctly detecting a true effect.

"One-sided vs two-sided?" → Two-sided is default; pick one-sided only if direction is fixed in advance.

"P-value interpretation?" → NOT P(H₀ true), NOT P(observed by chance), NOT P(reproducible).

"Statistical vs practical significance?" → Big n makes trivial effects significant; report effect size too.

"Multiple comparison correction?" → Bonferroni (divide α by k) or FDR (Benjamini-Hochberg).

"CI / p-value duality?" → Two-sided p < 0.05 ↔ μ₀ outside 95% CI.

"Failed to reject means?" → NOT "accept H₀"; just "not enough evidence to reject."

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • H₀ is the default/boring claim; H₁ is what you'd need evidence to support
  • p-value: probability of seeing data this extreme (or more) if H₀ were true
  • Decision rule: reject H₀ when p < α (typically α = 0.05)
  • "Fail to reject" ≠ "accept H₀" — absence of evidence isn't proof
  • Type I error (α) = reject true H₀ (false positive)
  • Type II error (β) = fail to reject false H₀ (false negative)
  • Power = 1 − β = chance of correctly detecting a true effect
  • Test statistic = (observed − null) / SE; how many SEs from the null value
  • Two-sided is default; one-sided only when direction is pre-specified by the problem's logic
  • CI / p-value duality: reject H₀: μ = μ₀ (two-sided α = 0.05) ↔ μ₀ outside 95% CI
  • Statistical significance ≠ practical importance — always report effect size or CI alongside p
  • Multiple comparisons inflate false positives — correct via Bonferroni or FDR
  • P-hacking, peeking, post-hoc one-sided tests all inflate Type I error rate — avoid
  • Five-step procedure: hypotheses → α → test statistic → p-value → decision + plain-English conclusion
📊 FIGURE — Rejection region, test statistic, and p-value
Under H₀, the test statistic follows this curve. The red tail beyond the critical value has area α (your false-alarm budget). If the observed statistic lands beyond it, the p-value (the tail area past YOUR statistic) is smaller than α — evidence rare enough to reject H₀.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The t-test is the most-used statistical test in the world. Any time you're comparing means — "is treatment better?", "did the change increase revenue?", "do these two groups differ?" — you're probably running some variant of a t-test. The DataCamp Data Scientist Associate exam tests all three forms (one-sample, two-sample, paired), and choosing the right one is the most common application-level error in practice.

Three flavors of t-test

TestComparesExample
One-sample t-testA sample mean to a known value"Is average response time different from 100ms?"
Two-sample t-test (independent)Means of TWO independent groupsA/B test, men vs women, treatment vs control
Paired t-testMeans of two MATCHED measurementsBefore/after on same subjects

One-sample t-test

ONE-SAMPLE T-TEST
Hypotheses:
  H₀: μ = μ₀
  H₁: μ ≠ μ₀ (or one-sided)

Test statistic:

t = (x̄ − μ₀) / (s / √n)

Compare to t-distribution with df = n − 1. 
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# Question: server response times — are they different from a target of 200ms?
sample = np.array([195, 210, 198, 220, 205, 215, 200, 225, 198, 218,
 208, 195, 230, 215, 200])

# Hypotheses (two-sided)
# H₀: μ = 200ms
# H₁: μ ≠ 200ms

result = stats.ttest_1samp(sample, popmean=200)
result.statistic # 2.39
result.pvalue # 0.0312

# p ≈ 0.031 < 0.05 → reject H₀
# Response times DO differ from 200ms (sample mean ≈ 209)

# One-sided version: are they GREATER than 200?
# H₁: μ > 200
result_one = stats.ttest_1samp(sample, popmean=200, alternative='greater')
# Half the two-sided p ≈ 0.0156 (if observation is in the predicted direction)
result_one.pvalue # ≈ 0.0156

# 'less' for the other direction

Assumptions of the one-sample t-test

  • Independent observations — no clustering, no time-series autocorrelation
  • Approximately normal data OR large n (CLT)
  • Continuous (interval/ratio) measurement — not for binary or categorical

Two-sample (independent) t-test

TWO-SAMPLE T-TEST
Hypotheses:
  H₀: μ₁ = μ₂
  H₁: μ₁ ≠ μ₂ (or one-sided)

Test statistic:

t = (x̄₁ − x̄₂) / SE(x̄₁ − x̄₂)

Two variants: Student's t (assumes equal variances) and Welch's t (does not).

Welch's t-test — the default to use

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# Treatment vs control test scores
control = np.array([75, 78, 82, 70, 85, 79, 73, 81, 77, 80])
treatment = np.array([82, 88, 90, 85, 91, 87, 84, 89, 86, 92])

# Welch's t-test (does NOT assume equal variances) — default in scipy
result = stats.ttest_ind(treatment, control, equal_var=False)
result.statistic # 5.94
result.pvalue # 0.000012

# Tiny p-value — strong evidence of difference
# Treatment mean: 87.4 — Control mean: 78.0 — diff ≈ 9.4

# Why Welch's? It doesn't require the two groups to have the same variance.
# In real data, equal variances rarely hold. Welch's is robust.

Student's t-test — when variances are known equal

# Student's t — assumes both groups have the same variance
# Slightly more statistical power if assumption holds; misleading otherwise

result = stats.ttest_ind(treatment, control, equal_var=True)
# Same statistic in this case because variances are similar
# But for groups with very different variances, results diverge

# To check the assumption: Levene's test
from scipy.stats import levene
levene_result = levene(treatment, control)
levene_result.pvalue # If > 0.05, variances are "equal enough"

# DEFAULT BEST PRACTICE: use Welch's (equal_var=False).
# It's the safer choice; modern packages default to Welch's where they can.

Paired t-test — matched measurements

PAIRED T-TEST
When two measurements come from the SAME unit (subject, item, day, etc.):
  • Compute differences d = x₁ − x₂ for each pair
  • Run a one-sample t-test on the differences (H₀: μ_d = 0)

Much more powerful than independent t-test when measurements within a pair are correlated. 
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# Before/after weights of 10 subjects on a new diet
before = np.array([180, 165, 195, 170, 175, 200, 185, 190, 178, 168])
after = np.array([175, 162, 188, 165, 170, 195, 180, 185, 175, 165])

# Paired t-test
result = stats.ttest_rel(before, after)
result.statistic # 7.50
result.pvalue # 3.6e-05

# Equivalent: compute the differences and one-sample t-test against 0
diffs = before - after
result2 = stats.ttest_1samp(diffs, popmean=0)
# Same answer

# Why this is BETTER than independent t-test:
# Subjects vary a lot from each other (180 vs 200 starting weight)
# But each one lost about 5 lbs
# Independent test compares 180 average to 175 average — small effect amid huge variance
# Paired test compares "each person to themselves" — same 5-lb shift but much less noise

When to use paired vs independent

SituationUse
Same subjects, before/afterPaired
Twins, sibling pairs, matched controlsPaired
Same store on two different daysPaired
A/B test: different users in each variantIndependent
Comparing male and female employeesIndependent
Treatment group vs control group (different people)Independent
⚠ USING THE WRONG ONE

Running an independent t-test when data are paired loses statistical power dramatically — you may fail to detect real effects.

Running a paired t-test when data are NOT paired produces nonsense — you're comparing arbitrary index-matched pairs.

The question to ask: "Is there a meaningful 1-to-1 relationship between the i-th value in group A and the i-th value in group B?"

Effect size — Cohen's d

COHEN'S d
A standardized measure of how much two means differ:

d = (x̄₁ − x̄₂) / s_pooled

Interpretation (Cohen's rough guidelines):
  |d| ≈ 0.2: small effect
  |d| ≈ 0.5: medium effect
  |d| ≈ 0.8: large effect

Report effect size ALONGSIDE p-value — it tells you the "how big" while p tells you "real or not." 
import numpy as np

control = np.array([75, 78, 82, 70, 85, 79, 73, 81, 77, 80])
treatment = np.array([82, 88, 90, 85, 91, 87, 84, 89, 86, 92])

# Cohen's d (pooled SD)
diff = treatment.mean() - control.mean()
n1, n2 = len(treatment), len(control)
s1, s2 = treatment.std(ddof=1), control.std(ddof=1)
pooled_sd = np.sqrt(((n1-1)*s1**2 + (n2-1)*s2**2) / (n1 + n2 - 2))

d = diff / pooled_sd # ≈ 2.66 — huge effect

# Reporting: "Treatment improved scores by 9.4 points (Cohen's d = 2.66, p < 0.001).
# The effect was very large by Cohen's conventions."

Non-parametric alternatives when t-test assumptions fail

Parametric t-testNon-parametric alternativeUse when
One-sample t-testWilcoxon signed-rankSkewed data, small n
Independent t-testMann-Whitney U (rank-sum)Skewed, ordinal, small n
Paired t-testWilcoxon signed-rank (on differences)Same conditions
 
from scipy import stats

# Mann-Whitney U (independent, non-parametric)
result = stats.mannwhitneyu(treatment, control, alternative='two-sided')

# Wilcoxon signed-rank (paired, non-parametric)
result = stats.wilcoxon(before, after)

# These tests rank the data and don't assume normality
# They have a bit less power than t-tests when t's assumptions DO hold
# But they're robust when normality fails

Worked example — full A/B test analysis

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Revenue A/B test

Scenario: Test a new pricing page. Compare average revenue per visitor (continuous outcome).

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

np.random.seed(42)
control = np.random.exponential(scale=10, size=500)
variant = np.random.exponential(scale=11, size=500)

# Step 1: examine the data
print(f"Control mean: {control.mean():.2f}, SD: {control.std(ddof=1):.2f}")
print(f"Variant mean: {variant.mean():.2f}, SD: {variant.std(ddof=1):.2f}")

# Step 2: visualize — exponential is right-skewed
# Means are valid because n is large (CLT) and we're comparing means, not modeling raw data

# Step 3: Welch's t-test (don't assume equal variances)
result = stats.ttest_ind(variant, control, equal_var=False)
print(f"t = {result.statistic:.3f}")
print(f"p = {result.pvalue:.4f}")
# p ~ 0.02 — significant at α = 0.05

# Step 4: effect size (Cohen's d on means)
diff = variant.mean() - control.mean()
pooled_sd = np.sqrt((control.var(ddof=1) + variant.var(ddof=1)) / 2)
d = diff / pooled_sd

# Step 5: CI for the difference
se_diff = np.sqrt(control.var(ddof=1)/500 + variant.var(ddof=1)/500)
ci = (diff - 1.96*se_diff, diff + 1.96*se_diff)

# Reporting
print(f"Variant lifts revenue by ${diff:.2f} per visitor (95% CI: {ci[0]:.2f} to {ci[1]:.2f})")
print(f"Cohen's d = {d:.3f} ({'small' if abs(d)<0.3 else 'medium' if abs(d)<0.6 else 'large'} effect)")
print(f"p-value = {result.pvalue:.4f}")
# Real-world conclusion: small but real lift; check whether it covers the rollout cost

Common t-test mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Using independent t-test for paired data — loses power; may miss real effects
  2. Using paired t-test on unrelated samples — produces meaningless statistics
  3. Assuming equal variances without checking — Student's t can mislead; Welch's is safer default
  4. Running t-test on counts or proportions — use the appropriate proportion/chi-square test instead
  5. Running on heavily skewed small samples — CLT hasn't kicked in; use non-parametric or transform
  6. Not reporting effect size — p-value alone is incomplete
  7. Forgetting that paired t-test df = n − 1, where n is PAIRS, not total observations
  8. Using one-sided test post-hoc — must be pre-specified
  9. Stopping the experiment as soon as p < 0.05 — sequential testing inflates Type I error
  10. Confusing scipy's ttest_ind vs ttest_rel vs ttest_1samp
★ ON THE EXAM

"One-sample t-test?" → Compare sample mean to a known value; stats.ttest_1samp(data, popmean=μ₀).

"Independent two-sample?" → Two unrelated groups; stats.ttest_ind(a, b, equal_var=False).

"Paired t-test?" → Two measurements per unit; stats.ttest_rel(before, after).

"Welch's vs Student's?" → Welch's (equal_var=False) is the safer default.

"df for one-sample?" → n − 1.

"df for Student's two-sample?" → n₁ + n₂ − 2.

"df for paired t-test?" → n − 1 where n is pairs.

"Non-parametric alternative to t-test?" → Mann-Whitney U (independent) or Wilcoxon signed-rank (paired/one-sample).

"Cohen's d ≈ 0.5?" → Medium effect; report alongside p-value.

"Best practice for variance assumption?" → Use Welch's t (equal_var=False) by default.

"Before/after data?" → Paired t-test.

"A/B test on different users?" → Independent t-test.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • t-tests compare means and assume approximately normal data (or large n via CLT)
  • One-sample: compare a single sample mean to a known value
  • Two-sample independent: compare means of two unrelated groups
  • Paired: compare two related measurements (same unit measured twice)
  • Welch's t-test (equal_var=False) is the modern default — works whether variances are equal or not
  • Paired t-test reduces to one-sample t-test on the differences
  • Using independent when paired data exists is the #1 application error — major loss of power
  • df = n − 1 (one-sample, paired), n₁ + n₂ − 2 (Student's), Welch-Satterthwaite (Welch's)
  • Always report Cohen's d (effect size) alongside the p-value
  • Non-parametric alternatives (Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon) when normality fails or n is small
  • Common scipy functions: ttest_1samp, ttest_ind, ttest_rel
  • Default to two-sided (alternative='two-sided'); only use one-sided when direction is pre-specified
  • Heavily skewed small samples: use non-parametric or log-transform first
📊 FIGURE — Rejection region, test statistic, and p-value
Under H₀, the test statistic follows this curve. The red tail beyond the critical value has area α (your false-alarm budget). If the observed statistic lands beyond it, the p-value (the tail area past YOUR statistic) is smaller than α — evidence rare enough to reject H₀.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The chi-square test is the go-to method for CATEGORICAL data — when you're counting observations across categories rather than averaging numerical values. It answers questions like "are these categories independent?" and "does our data match an expected distribution?". The DataCamp Data Scientist Associate exam tests both the goodness-of-fit and test of independence forms, plus the assumptions.

Two main chi-square tests

TestQuestionData shape
Goodness-of-fitDoes observed match expected distribution?1 categorical variable with counts
Test of independenceAre two categorical variables independent?Contingency table (2 categorical variables)

The chi-square statistic — same formula for both

CHI-SQUARE STATISTIC

χ² = Σ [(O − E)² / E]

Sum across all cells of (Observed − Expected)² / Expected.

Compare to a chi-square distribution with appropriate df.
Large χ² → big mismatch between observed and expected → reject H₀.

Chi-square goodness-of-fit test

GOODNESS-OF-FIT
H₀: the data follows the specified distribution.
H₁: it doesn't.

Degrees of freedom: df = (number of categories) − 1 − (estimated parameters) 
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# Example: is a die fair?
# Rolled 120 times. Counts per face:
observed = [22, 17, 20, 26, 22, 13]

# Under H₀ (fair die): each face equally likely → expected = 120/6 = 20 each
expected = [20, 20, 20, 20, 20, 20]

# Chi-square statistic
chi2 = sum((o - e)**2 / e for o, e in zip(observed, expected))
# = 4 + 9 + 0 + 36 + 4 + 49 over 20s
# ≈ 5.10

# df = 6 - 1 = 5 (6 categories, all 0 parameters estimated)
p_value = 1 - stats.chi2.cdf(5.10, df=5)
# ≈ 0.404 — no evidence to reject fairness

# Or just call scipy directly
result = stats.chisquare(f_obs=observed, f_exp=expected)
result.statistic # 5.10
result.pvalue # 0.404
# Same answer with one line

# Conclusion: with p > 0.05, we fail to reject H₀
# The die data is consistent with a fair die

Goodness-of-fit with non-uniform expected probabilities

# Example: do customers' product preferences match prior year's distribution?
# Prior year: A 50%, B 30%, C 20%
# This year, out of 500 customers:
observed = [220, 180, 100] # A, B, C

# Expected under H₀ (same distribution as last year)
expected_props = [0.50, 0.30, 0.20]
expected = [p * 500 for p in expected_props] # [250, 150, 100]

result = stats.chisquare(f_obs=observed, f_exp=expected)
# χ² ≈ 9.6, p ≈ 0.0082
# REJECT H₀ — distribution has shifted (more B, less A)

Goodness-of-fit assumptions

  • Independent observations: same as t-tests — no double-counting
  • Expected counts ≥ 5 in each cell (some sources say ≥ 1 in most cells, with no cell < 5)
  • Sample size large enough: rule of thumb n ≥ 5 × number of categories

Chi-square test of independence

TEST OF INDEPENDENCE
H₀: the two categorical variables are INDEPENDENT.
H₁: they are associated (not independent).

Expected count for cell (i, j) under independence:
  Eij = (row total i × column total j) / grand total

df = (rows − 1) × (cols − 1) 
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

# Survey: 500 people asked about political party + age group
# Observed counts:
# Dem Rep Ind
# 18-34 110 50 40
# 35-54 80 100 30
# 55+ 40 100 50

observed = np.array([
 [110, 50, 40],
 [ 80, 100, 30],
 [ 40, 100, 50]
])

# Chi-square test of independence
result = stats.chi2_contingency(observed)
chi2 = result.statistic # 67.7
p_value = result.pvalue # ~2e-13
df = result.dof # (3-1)*(3-1) = 4
expected = result.expected_freq

# Tiny p — strongly reject independence
# Party preference IS related to age group

# Examine expected vs observed to see WHERE the differences are
print(pd.DataFrame(observed - expected))

Setting up a contingency table from raw data

import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

# Suppose you have individual-level data
df = pd.DataFrame({
 'age_group': ['18-34', '18-34', '35-54', '55+', ...],
 'party': ['Dem', 'Rep', 'Ind', 'Rep', ...]
})

# Build contingency table with pandas
ct = pd.crosstab(df['age_group'], df['party'])

# Apply chi-square test of independence
result = stats.chi2_contingency(ct)
print(f"χ² = {result.statistic:.2f}, df = {result.dof}, p = {result.pvalue:.4f}")

Reading the expected-frequency table

# The "expected" frequencies are what you'd see if the variables were truly independent
# Compared to observed, you can see WHICH cells deviate the most

# For 2x2 tables:
# Outcome+ Outcome- | Total
# Group A 50 150 200
# Group B 30 170 200
# 80 320 400

# Expected under independence:
# E(A, +) = (200 × 80) / 400 = 40
# E(A, -) = (200 × 320) / 400 = 160
# E(B, +) = (200 × 80) / 400 = 40
# E(B, -) = (200 × 320) / 400 = 160

# Observed: 50, 150, 30, 170
# Expected: 40, 160, 40, 160
# A has MORE positives than expected; B has FEWER → suggests an association

import numpy as np
observed = np.array(5015030170)
result = stats.chi2_contingency(observed)
# χ² ≈ 6.25, df = 1, p ≈ 0.012 → significant association

The 2x2 special case — Fisher's exact test

★ WHEN SAMPLE IS SMALL

For 2x2 tables with small expected counts (any cell < 5), use Fisher's exact test instead of chi-square.

Fisher's exact computes the exact probability under H₀ using the hypergeometric distribution — no approximation.

from scipy.stats import fisher_exact
table = 5127
odds_ratio, p_value = fisher_exact(table)
# Works for any cell counts; doesn't need expected ≥ 5 rule

Continuity correction (Yates' correction)

# For 2x2 tables, some statisticians apply Yates' correction:
# χ² = Σ [(|O - E| - 0.5)² / E]
# Reduces over-rejection in small samples

# In scipy, this is the default for 2x2 tables in chi2_contingency:
result = stats.chi2_contingency(observed) # Yates' correction applied automatically
result = stats.chi2_contingency(observed, correction=False) # disable

# For larger tables, no correction needed

Effect size for chi-square — Cramér's V

CRAMÉR'S V

V = √(χ² / (n × min(rows−1, cols−1)))

Ranges 0 (no association) to 1 (perfect association).

Interpretation (Cohen's rough guidelines, varies by table size):
  V ≈ 0.1: small effect
  V ≈ 0.3: medium effect
  V ≈ 0.5+: large effect 
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

observed = np.array([
 [110, 50, 40],
 [ 80, 100, 30],
 [ 40, 100, 50]
])

result = stats.chi2_contingency(observed)
n = observed.sum()
min_dim = min(observed.shape[0]-1, observed.shape[1]-1)
cramers_v = np.sqrt(result.statistic / (n * min_dim))
# ≈ 0.26 — small-to-medium association

# Always report along with p-value:
# "Significant association detected (χ² = 67.7, df = 4, p < 0.001, Cramér's V = 0.26).
# Effect size is small-to-medium."

Chi-square test for proportions (two groups)

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# A/B test: did variant convert at a different rate than control?
# Control: 250 conversions out of 5000 = 5.0%
# Variant: 300 conversions out of 5000 = 6.0%

# 2x2 table: [converted, not converted] x [control, variant]
table = np.array([
 [250, 4750], # control
 [300, 4700] # variant
])

result = stats.chi2_contingency(table)
# χ² ≈ 4.93, df = 1, p ≈ 0.026
# REJECT H₀ — significant difference in conversion rates

# Equivalent to a z-test for two proportions
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportions_ztest
counts = np.array([250, 300])
nobs = np.array([5000, 5000])
z, p = proportions_ztest(counts, nobs)
# z ≈ -2.28, p ≈ 0.023 — same p-value (chi-square = z²)

Chi-square assumptions and conditions

⚠ CHI-SQUARE CONDITIONS
  1. Independent observations — same as all standard tests
  2. Counts, not percentages — chi-square requires raw integer counts
  3. Expected count ≥ 5 in each cell — common rule; some say ≥ 1 with at most 20% below 5
  4. For 2x2 with small cells: use Fisher's exact test
  5. Random sample from population

Worked example — full chi-square analysis

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Is gender associated with product preference?

Scenario: Survey 1000 customers. Tabulate preferred product by gender.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

# Survey results — contingency table
observed = np.array([
 [180, 120, 50], # Male: prefers A, B, C
 [200, 250, 200] # Female: prefers A, B, C
])

# Step 1: hypotheses
# H₀: gender and product preference are independent
# H₁: they are associated

# Step 2: test
result = stats.chi2_contingency(observed)
chi2, p, dof, expected = result.statistic, result.pvalue, result.dof, result.expected_freq

print(f"χ² = {chi2:.2f}") # 76.4
print(f"df = {dof}") # 2
print(f"p = {p:.6f}") # tiny

# Step 3: which cells deviate most?
residuals = (observed - expected) / np.sqrt(expected)
print("Standardized residuals:")
print(pd.DataFrame(residuals,
 index=['Male', 'Female'],
 columns=['A', 'B', 'C']))
# Male more often prefer A; female more often prefer C
# Magnitudes >|2| suggest meaningful deviation

# Step 4: effect size
n = observed.sum()
cramers_v = np.sqrt(chi2 / (n * min(observed.shape[0]-1, observed.shape[1]-1)))
print(f"Cramér's V = {cramers_v:.3f}") # ≈ 0.28

# Reporting:
# "Gender and product preference are significantly associated
# (χ² = 76.4, df = 2, p < 0.001, Cramér's V = 0.28).
# Males prefer A more than expected; females prefer C more than expected."

Common chi-square mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Running chi-square on PERCENTAGES not counts — must use raw integer counts
  2. Expected counts < 5 in cells — switch to Fisher's exact
  3. Counting the same subject in multiple cells — violates independence (e.g., multiple purchases per customer)
  4. Confusing observed marginal totals with population proportions
  5. Not reporting effect size (Cramér's V) — large samples make tiny associations significant
  6. Treating large χ² as automatically meaningful — check effect size for practical significance
  7. Using chi-square for paired categorical data — use McNemar's test instead
  8. Ignoring Yates' correction for 2x2 — scipy applies it automatically; some sources don't
  9. Wrong df — for goodness-of-fit, df = categories − 1; for independence, df = (r−1)(c−1)
  10. Comparing groups of very different sizes without checking expected counts
★ ON THE EXAM

"Chi-square goodness-of-fit?" → Tests if observed matches expected distribution. df = categories − 1.

"Chi-square test of independence?" → Tests if two categorical variables are independent. df = (r−1)(c−1).

"Chi-square statistic formula?" → Σ (O − E)² / E.

"Expected count under independence?" → (row total × column total) / grand total.

"Required cell count?" → Expected ≥ 5 in (most) cells.

"Small cell counts?" → Use Fisher's exact test.

"Chi-square needs counts, not?" → Percentages or proportions — always raw counts.

"Effect size?" → Cramér's V (0=none, 1=perfect).

"Paired categorical data?" → McNemar's test (not chi-square).

"2x2 with continuity correction?" → Yates' correction; default in scipy.

"scipy.stats.chi2_contingency returns?" → χ² statistic, p-value, df, expected frequencies.

"goodness-of-fit in scipy?" → stats.chisquare(f_obs, f_exp).

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Chi-square works on categorical data (counts), not continuous data
  • Goodness-of-fit: does observed match expected distribution? df = categories − 1
  • Test of independence: are two categorical variables related? df = (rows − 1)(cols − 1)
  • Statistic: χ² = Σ (O − E)² / E across all cells
  • Expected counts under independence: (row total × column total) / grand total
  • Conditions: independent observations, raw counts (not percentages), expected ≥ 5 per cell
  • For 2x2 with small expected counts, use Fisher's exact test instead
  • 2x2 tables get Yates' continuity correction by default in scipy
  • Effect size: Cramér's V — ranges 0 to 1; report alongside p-value
  • Chi-square test on 2x2 is equivalent to a two-proportion z-test (chi² = z²)
  • For paired categorical data (before/after preferences), use McNemar's test
  • scipy functions: chi2_contingency (independence), chisquare (goodness-of-fit), fisher_exact (small 2x2)
  • Build contingency tables from raw data with pd.crosstab
  • With large n, chi-square detects tiny associations as "significant" — always check Cramér's V for practical importance
📊 FIGURE — Chi-square: observed vs. expected counts
For each category, compare the observed count (indigo) with what the null hypothesis expects (outline): χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E. Big mismatches inflate χ²; if it exceeds the critical value for the right degrees of freedom, the hypothesized distribution is rejected.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

ANOVA (Analysis of Variance) tests whether THREE OR MORE groups have the same mean. You can't just run multiple t-tests (multiple-comparison problem inflates false positives). ANOVA gives you a single test for "do any of these groups differ?" The DataCamp Data Scientist Associate exam tests one-way ANOVA setup, interpretation, post-hoc tests, and assumptions.

Why not just run multiple t-tests?

# Suppose you want to compare means across 4 groups.
# Pairwise t-tests would require C(4, 2) = 6 separate tests.

# If all nulls are TRUE and α = 0.05 per test:
# P(at least one false positive) = 1 - (0.95)^6 ≈ 0.265
# 26.5% chance of falsely "finding a difference" — way above 5%.

# ANOVA tests ALL groups in ONE test at α = 0.05:
# Overall false positive rate stays at 5%.

# Then, IF ANOVA is significant, run post-hoc pairwise tests WITH CORRECTION
# to pinpoint which specific groups differ.

One-way ANOVA — the basic test

ONE-WAY ANOVA
Compares means across k groups defined by ONE categorical predictor.

H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ = ... = μ_k (all group means equal)
H₁: at least one group mean differs

Test statistic: F = (between-group variance) / (within-group variance)
Compare to F-distribution with df1 = k − 1 and df2 = N − k. 
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# Three teaching methods, 10 students each, test score outcome
method_a = np.array([78, 82, 75, 80, 85, 79, 81, 77, 83, 80])
method_b = np.array([88, 92, 85, 90, 87, 91, 89, 86, 93, 88])
method_c = np.array([80, 78, 82, 85, 79, 81, 84, 80, 83, 78])

result = stats.f_oneway(method_a, method_b, method_c)
result.statistic # F ≈ 25.4
result.pvalue # ≈ 1.2e-07

# Tiny p-value → reject H₀: methods differ
# But ANOVA doesn't tell you WHICH methods differ — you need post-hoc tests for that

What the F-statistic captures

F-STATISTIC INTUITION

F = MS_between / MS_within

Between-group variance: how spread out the group MEANS are.
Within-group variance: how spread out individuals are WITHIN their group.

When group means are similar (relative to within-group noise) → F near 1.
When group means differ a lot → F much greater than 1 → reject H₀. 
import numpy as np

# Compute F by hand to understand it
groups = [method_a, method_b, method_c]
n_per = [len(g) for g in groups]
grand_mean = np.mean(np.concatenate(groups))
group_means = [g.mean() for g in groups]

# Sum of squares between (SSB)
ssb = sum(n * (m - grand_mean)**2 for n, m in zip(n_per, group_means))

# Sum of squares within (SSW)
ssw = sum(((g - g.mean())**2).sum() for g in groups)

# Degrees of freedom
k = len(groups)
N = sum(n_per)
df_between = k - 1 # 2
df_within = N - k # 27

# Mean squares
ms_between = ssb / df_between
ms_within = ssw / df_within

# F
F = ms_between / ms_within # ≈ 25.4 — matches scipy

Post-hoc tests — finding WHICH groups differ

import pandas as pd
from statsmodels.stats.multicomp import pairwise_tukeyhsd

# Combine data into long format
data = pd.DataFrame({
 'score': np.concatenate([method_a, method_b, method_c]),
 'method': ['A']*10 + ['B']*10 + ['C']*10
})

# Tukey HSD test (Honestly Significant Difference)
tukey = pairwise_tukeyhsd(endog=data['score'], groups=data['method'], alpha=0.05)
print(tukey)
# Pairwise comparisons with adjusted p-values:
# A vs B: significant (large difference)
# A vs C: not significant
# B vs C: significant
# So B is the odd one out — both A and C differ from B, but A doesn't differ from C

# Tukey's HSD controls family-wise error rate across all pairwise comparisons
# Preferred over running Bonferroni-corrected t-tests for ANOVA follow-up

# Alternative: Bonferroni-corrected pairwise t-tests
from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests
# Run pairwise t-tests, then correct p-values

Assumptions of ANOVA

AssumptionCheck
Independent observationsSame as all tests
Normality within groupsQ-Q plot per group; Shapiro-Wilk. Robust for moderate-large n.
Equal variances across groups (homoscedasticity)Levene's test or Bartlett's test
 
from scipy.stats import levene, bartlett

# Test equal variance assumption
levene_result = levene(method_a, method_b, method_c)
levene_result.pvalue # > 0.05 → variances OK to assume equal

# If variances differ, use Welch's ANOVA (the one-way ANOVA equivalent of Welch's t-test)
# scipy: stats.f_oneway assumes equal variances
# For Welch's: use pingouin or scipy.stats.f_oneway with care

# pingouin makes Welch's easy:
# import pingouin as pg
# pg.welch_anova(data=df, dv='score', between='method')

Non-parametric alternative — Kruskal-Wallis

from scipy.stats import kruskal

# When normality assumption fails or data is ordinal
result = kruskal(method_a, method_b, method_c)
result.statistic
result.pvalue

# Like ANOVA but ranks the data first — no normality needed
# Less power than ANOVA when normality holds; more robust otherwise

Effect size for ANOVA — eta squared

ETA SQUARED (η²)

η² = SS_between / SS_total

Proportion of total variance explained by group membership. Ranges 0 to 1.

Cohen's conventions:
  η² ≈ 0.01: small effect
  η² ≈ 0.06: medium effect
  η² ≈ 0.14: large effect 
ss_total = ssb + ssw
eta_squared = ssb / ss_total
# ≈ 0.65 — large effect; 65% of variance in test scores is explained by teaching method

# Always report effect size with the F and p value

Two-way ANOVA — two categorical predictors

import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
import statsmodels.api as sm

# Effects of teaching method AND class size on test scores
# H₀ for method: no main effect of method
# H₀ for size: no main effect of class size
# H₀ for interaction: method and size don't interact

model = smf.ols('score ~ C(method) + C(size) + C(method):C(size)', data=df).fit()
table = sm.stats.anova_lm(model, typ=2)
print(table)
# sum_sq df F PR(>F)
# C(method) ... 2 25.40 ...
# C(size) ... 1 ... ...
# C(method):C(size) ... 2 ... ...
# Residual ... 24 ... NaN

# Three F-tests in one analysis:
# Main effect of method
# Main effect of class size
# Interaction: does the effect of method DEPEND on class size?

Interactions — when group differences depend on a second variable

★ WHAT AN INTERACTION MEANS

"Method A is best in small classes; Method B is best in large classes" — that's an interaction. The effect of one factor depends on the level of another.

If the interaction term is significant, you can't talk meaningfully about the "main effect" of either factor in isolation — they're entangled.

Visualize with an interaction plot: x = factor 1, y = mean outcome, separate lines for factor 2.

import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Interaction plot
sns.pointplot(data=df, x='method', y='score', hue='size')
# Parallel lines = no interaction
# Crossing or diverging lines = interaction present

Repeated measures ANOVA — paired-data version

# When the same subjects are measured at multiple time points or conditions
# (e.g., test score before/middle/after training — same students)

# Use pingouin or statsmodels for repeated-measures
# import pingouin as pg
# pg.rm_anova(data=df, dv='score', within='time', subject='subject_id')

# More powerful than running independent ANOVA because it controls for between-subject differences
# Same logic as paired t-test extending to 3+ time points

Worked example — full ANOVA workflow

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Comparing 4 marketing channels

Scenario: Test conversion rates across 4 ad channels. Each channel ran 30 days. Daily conversion counts are recorded.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
from statsmodels.stats.multicomp import pairwise_tukeyhsd

# Simulated data
np.random.seed(42)
fb = np.random.normal(loc=50, scale=10, size=30)
google = np.random.normal(loc=55, scale=10, size=30)
tiktok = np.random.normal(loc=65, scale=10, size=30)
email = np.random.normal(loc=48, scale=10, size=30)

# Step 1: hypotheses
# H₀: μ_fb = μ_google = μ_tiktok = μ_email
# H₁: at least one differs

# Step 2: check assumptions
print(stats.levene(fb, google, tiktok, email).pvalue)
# > 0.05 → variances roughly equal — ANOVA OK

# Step 3: one-way ANOVA
result = stats.f_oneway(fb, google, tiktok, email)
print(f"F = {result.statistic:.2f}, p = {result.pvalue:.4f}")
# F ≈ 13.7, p < 0.001 → reject H₀ — at least one channel differs

# Step 4: effect size
all_data = np.concatenate([fb, google, tiktok, email])
grand_mean = all_data.mean()
group_means = [fb.mean(), google.mean(), tiktok.mean(), email.mean()]
ssb = sum(30 * (m - grand_mean)**2 for m in group_means)
sst = ((all_data - grand_mean)**2).sum()
eta_sq = ssb / sst
print(f"η² = {eta_sq:.3f}") # ≈ 0.26 — large effect

# Step 5: post-hoc — which channels differ?
data = pd.DataFrame({
 'conversions': all_data,
 'channel': ['FB']*30 + ['Google']*30 + ['TikTok']*30 + ['Email']*30
})
tukey = pairwise_tukeyhsd(data['conversions'], data['channel'])
print(tukey.summary())
# Likely: TikTok significantly higher than all others; FB ~ Google ~ Email

# Reporting:
# "Channels differ significantly (F(3, 116) = 13.7, p < 0.001, η² = 0.26).
# Tukey HSD identifies TikTok as significantly higher than FB, Google, and Email.
# The other three channels do not significantly differ from each other."

Common ANOVA mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Running multiple t-tests instead of ANOVA — inflates Type I error rate
  2. Running ANOVA without checking equal variances — use Levene's test first; Welch's ANOVA if violated
  3. Concluding from a significant ANOVA without post-hoc — F-test says "at least one differs"; post-hoc says which
  4. Using uncorrected pairwise t-tests after significant ANOVA — inflates false positives; use Tukey HSD
  5. Treating repeated-measures data as independent — paired/repeated-measures ANOVA preserves within-subject information
  6. Interpreting main effects when interaction is significant — they're entangled
  7. Not reporting effect size (η²) — F-statistic with large n can be tiny effect
  8. Skipping ANOVA when k = 2 — fine, but ANOVA with k = 2 is equivalent to a t-test
  9. Forgetting df — F has TWO degrees of freedom (between, within)
★ ON THE EXAM

"ANOVA tests?" → Whether 3+ group means are all equal.

"H₀?" → All group means equal: μ₁ = μ₂ = ... = μ_k.

"H₁?" → At least one group mean differs.

"F-statistic?" → MS_between / MS_within; F ≈ 1 under H₀, larger when groups differ.

"Why ANOVA instead of pairwise t-tests?" → Controls family-wise Type I error rate.

"df for one-way ANOVA?" → (k − 1, N − k).

"Significant ANOVA — next step?" → Post-hoc test (Tukey HSD).

"Effect size?" → η² (eta squared) = SS_between / SS_total.

"Assumptions?" → Independence, normality within groups, equal variances.

"Variances differ?" → Use Welch's ANOVA.

"Non-parametric alternative?" → Kruskal-Wallis test.

"Same subjects over time?" → Repeated-measures ANOVA (paired analog).

"Two-way ANOVA?" → Two categorical predictors; tests main effects + interaction.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • ANOVA tests if 3+ group means are all equal — one test instead of many pairwise t-tests
  • F-statistic = between-group variance ÷ within-group variance
  • F ≈ 1 under H₀; large F → reject H₀
  • df: between = k − 1, within = N − k
  • Assumptions: independent observations, normal-ish data within groups, equal variances across groups
  • Check equal variances with Levene's; use Welch's ANOVA if violated
  • Significant ANOVA tells you SOMETHING differs but not WHICH groups — run post-hoc tests
  • Tukey HSD is the standard post-hoc for finding pairwise differences
  • Effect size: η² (eta squared) = SS_between / SS_total; 0.01 small, 0.06 medium, 0.14 large
  • Two-way ANOVA includes two predictors + their interaction
  • Interactions: effect of one factor depends on level of another — visualize with interaction plot
  • Repeated-measures ANOVA handles within-subject correlation (same units at multiple time points)
  • Non-parametric alternative: Kruskal-Wallis (then Dunn's post-hoc)
  • scipy: stats.f_oneway; statsmodels: anova_lm; post-hoc: pairwise_tukeyhsd
📊 FIGURE — ANOVA: is the spread BETWEEN groups big vs. the spread WITHIN?
Three groups of dots with their means (bars). ANOVA’s F statistic compares between-group variance (how far the means sit apart) to within-group variance (the scatter inside each strip). Large F ⇒ at least one mean differs; post-hoc tests find which.

📘 Deep dive: A/B testing end to end

An A/B test compares two variants — A the control, B the treatment — on a primary metric. Random assignment makes the groups comparable on average, eliminating confounding. Decide the sample size BEFORE the test via power analysis, and pick one primary metric in advance — multiple metrics inflate false positives.
