◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Correlation measures how strongly two variables move together — does X go up when Y goes up? It's the gateway to regression, the foundation of feature selection, and the most-used summary statistic in exploratory analysis. The DataCamp Data Scientist Associate exam tests Pearson vs Spearman, the −1 to 1 range, and the most-repeated catch: correlation is not causation.

Pearson correlation — the linear measure

PEARSON CORRELATION COEFFICIENT

r = Cov(X, Y) / (σ_X × σ_Y)

Standardized covariance.

Range: −1 to +1.
  r = +1: perfect positive LINEAR relationship
  r = −1: perfect negative linear
  r = 0: no LINEAR relationship (but possibly nonlinear) 
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

# Example: height and weight
height = np.array([60, 62, 65, 67, 68, 70, 72, 74, 76])
weight = np.array([110, 115, 130, 145, 150, 160, 175, 180, 195])

# scipy
r, p = stats.pearsonr(height, weight)
# r ≈ 0.996, p ≈ 1.4e-09 — strong positive correlation

# NumPy
np.corrcoef(height, weight)
# Returns 2x2 correlation matrix; [0,1] is the correlation

# Pandas — works on DataFrames
df = pd.DataFrame({'height': height, 'weight': weight})
df.corr() # full correlation matrix
df['height'].corr(df['weight']) # single pair

Interpreting r magnitudes

|r|Strength
0.0 – 0.1Essentially none
0.1 – 0.3Weak
0.3 – 0.5Moderate
0.5 – 0.7Strong
0.7 – 1.0Very strong

These bands vary by field — social sciences treat r = 0.3 as strong; physics expects r > 0.95.

Spearman correlation — for ranks

SPEARMAN'S RANK CORRELATION
Pearson correlation computed on the RANKS of the data, not the raw values.

Captures any MONOTONIC relationship (X and Y move in the same direction, even if not linearly).
Robust to outliers; insensitive to monotonic transformations. 
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# Pearson vs Spearman on data with an outlier
x = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 100])
y = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6])

pearson_r, _ = stats.pearsonr(x, y)
# ≈ 0.71 — outlier pulls down the linear correlation

spearman_r, _ = stats.spearmanr(x, y)
# ≈ 1.0 — ranks are still in perfect order

# Pandas
df.corr(method='spearman')

# Use Spearman when:
# • Data has outliers
# • Relationship is nonlinear but monotonic
# • Data is ordinal (ranks, ratings)
# • You don't want to assume normality

Pearson vs Spearman side-by-side

AspectPearsonSpearman
CapturesLinear relationshipsMonotonic relationships
Affected by outliersYesNo (works on ranks)
Requires normalityFor significance testNo
Data typeInterval/ratioAny ordered (incl. ordinal)
Use caseDefault for continuous numericSkewed data, outliers, ordinal

r squared — variance explained

R²
r² (coefficient of determination) = proportion of variance in Y explained by X.

Range 0 to 1. Useful when interpreting magnitude:
  r = 0.5 → r² = 0.25 → only 25% of variance explained
  r = 0.7 → r² = 0.49 → 49%
  r = 0.9 → r² = 0.81 → 81%

A correlation of 0.5 sounds "moderate" but only explains a quarter of the variance.

Statistical significance of a correlation

from scipy import stats

# scipy returns the p-value alongside r
r, p = stats.pearsonr(x, y)

# H₀: ρ = 0 (no linear relationship in the population)
# H₁: ρ ≠ 0
# p < 0.05 → reject H₀ → significant correlation

# With large n, even tiny r values can be "significant"
# Example: n = 100,000, r = 0.05 — p < 0.001, but only 0.25% variance explained
# ALWAYS REPORT BOTH r AND p (and ideally a CI for r)

Confidence interval for a correlation

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# Fisher's z-transform: stabilizes the sampling distribution of r
def correlation_ci(r, n, alpha=0.05):
 z = 0.5 * np.log((1 + r) / (1 - r)) # Fisher z
 se = 1 / np.sqrt(n - 3)
 z_crit = stats.norm.ppf(1 - alpha/2)
 z_lo = z - z_crit * se
 z_hi = z + z_crit * se
 # Back-transform
 r_lo = (np.exp(2*z_lo) - 1) / (np.exp(2*z_lo) + 1)
 r_hi = (np.exp(2*z_hi) - 1) / (np.exp(2*z_hi) + 1)
 return r_lo, r_hi

# CI for r = 0.5 with n = 30
correlation_ci(0.5, 30)
# ≈ (0.179, 0.731) — wide interval at this sample size

# Wider intervals when n is small or r is near 0
# Pingouin has this built in: pg.corr(x, y, ci=95)

Correlation matrices and heatmaps

import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns

# Multi-variable correlation matrix
df.corr() # Pearson by default
df.corr(method='spearman')
df.corr(method='kendall') # alternative rank-based correlation

# Heatmap visualization
sns.heatmap(df.corr(), annot=True, cmap='RdBu_r', center=0, vmin=-1, vmax=1)

# Look for:
# • High correlations between predictors (multicollinearity) — covered in ch6/s3
# • Strong predictor-target correlations (feature importance hint)
# • Unexpected correlations (data quality issues)

Correlation is NOT causation

⚠ THE MOST-REPEATED LESSON IN STATS

A correlation between X and Y can have many explanations:

  1. X causes Y — what you usually hope
  2. Y causes X — reverse causation
  3. Z causes both — confounder / lurking variable
  4. Selection bias — the sample is filtered in a way that creates the correlation
  5. Pure coincidence — especially with small n or many tested pairs

Classic example: ice cream sales correlate with drowning deaths. Z = hot weather causes both.

To establish causation: randomized controlled experiment, careful natural experiments (instrumental variables), or theory-driven causal modeling.

Anscombe's quartet — why visualization matters

★ FOUR DATASETS, SAME r

Anscombe's quartet is four datasets that all share:

  • Same mean of x and y
  • Same variance of x and y
  • Same Pearson r ≈ 0.816
  • Same r² and regression line

But they look TOTALLY different when plotted: linear trend, curve, outlier-driven, one influential point. Always plot your data — don't trust a single correlation number.

When correlation breaks down

Nonlinear relationships

import numpy as np

x = np.linspace(-3, 3, 100)
y = x**2

# Pearson r ≈ 0 — even though y is a perfect function of x
# The relationship is symmetric, not monotonic, so Pearson misses it
# Spearman also picks up little because of the symmetry

# Always plot your data — a 0 correlation doesn't mean "no relationship"

Outliers can flip correlation

x = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
y = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
stats.pearsonr(x, y) # r = 1.0

# Add one outlier
x2 = np.append(x, 100)
y2 = np.append(y, 0)
stats.pearsonr(x2, y2) # r ≈ -0.5 — flipped sign!

# Spearman is more robust:
stats.spearmanr(x2, y2) # still positive but reduced

Worked example — correlation analysis

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Customer data exploration

Scenario: Analyze relationships among customer age, income, and lifetime value.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

# Create example data
np.random.seed(0)
age = np.random.uniform(20, 70, 200)
income = 30000 + 1000 * age + np.random.normal(0, 10000, 200)
ltv = 100 + 0.01 * income + np.random.normal(0, 500, 200)

df = pd.DataFrame({'age': age, 'income': income, 'ltv': ltv})

# Pearson matrix
print(df.corr())
# age income ltv
# age 1.000 0.918 0.728
# income 0.918 1.000 0.797
# ltv 0.728 0.797 1.000

# Significance test for each pair
for col1, col2 in [('age', 'income'), ('age', 'ltv'), ('income', 'ltv')]:
 r, p = stats.pearsonr(df[col1], df[col2])
 print(f"{col1} vs {col2}: r = {r:.3f}, p = {p:.4f}")

# Visualize — Anscombe's lesson, always plot
sns.pairplot(df, kind='scatter')
plt.show()

# Heatmap of full correlation matrix
sns.heatmap(df.corr(), annot=True, cmap='RdBu_r', center=0)

# Interpretation:
# Strong age-income correlation (0.92) — older customers have higher income
# Moderate-strong income-LTV (0.80) — wealthier customers spend more
# Moderate age-LTV (0.73) — likely driven by age → income → LTV chain
# CAREFUL: don't conclude "age causes LTV" — income is a clear mediator

Common correlation mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Concluding causation from correlation — the cardinal sin
  2. Using Pearson with non-linear relationships — switch to Spearman or plot first
  3. Reporting r without r² — r = 0.5 sounds moderate but only 25% variance explained
  4. Treating r = 0 as "no relationship" — could be a nonlinear pattern
  5. Ignoring outliers — single points can flip the sign
  6. Tiny effect with huge n still flagged as significant — report effect size
  7. Multiple correlation tests without correction — running 50 pairs at α = 0.05 gives ~2-3 false positives
  8. Spurious correlations from time series trends — both variables drifting upward over time → correlated even if unrelated
  9. Mixing data types — Pearson on binary or categorical needs care (point-biserial, phi coefficient)
  10. Not plotting before correlating — Anscombe's quartet warning
★ ON THE EXAM

"Pearson r range?" → −1 to +1.

"r = 0 means?" → No LINEAR relationship (nonlinear still possible).

"r² interpretation?" → Proportion of variance in Y explained by X.

"Pearson vs Spearman?" → Pearson is linear; Spearman is monotonic (uses ranks).

"Outliers present?" → Spearman is robust; Pearson is not.

"Correlation matrix in pandas?" → df.corr(); method='pearson' (default), 'spearman', 'kendall'.

"Heatmap?" → sns.heatmap(df.corr()).

"H₀ for correlation test?" → ρ = 0.

"r = 0.5 — strong?" → Moderate-strong; explains 25% of variance.

"Correlation = causation?" → No. Could be reverse causation, confounding, or coincidence.

"Anscombe's quartet?" → Same r but different shapes — always plot data.

"Correlation needs?" → Independent observations, paired data, continuous-ish variables.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Correlation measures linear (Pearson) or monotonic (Spearman) association between two variables
  • r ranges from −1 to +1; sign = direction, magnitude = strength
  • r² = proportion of variance explained (more interpretable than r for magnitude)
  • Pearson assumes linearity and is sensitive to outliers; Spearman uses ranks and is robust
  • r = 0 means no LINEAR relationship — there could still be a nonlinear one (always plot)
  • Anscombe's quartet: four datasets with identical r but totally different shapes — plot before trusting r
  • Correlation tests use H₀: ρ = 0; scipy and pandas report p-values
  • With huge n, tiny correlations become "significant" but aren't practically meaningful — report both r and p
  • Correlation ≠ causation; alternatives include reverse causation, confounding, selection bias, coincidence
  • Correlation matrix + heatmap is the standard exploratory visualization for multi-variable datasets
  • Use Spearman when data is skewed, has outliers, or is ordinal
  • For categorical-numeric pairs: point-biserial or eta-squared
  • For two binary variables: phi coefficient or odds ratio
  • scipy: pearsonr, spearmanr, kendalltau; pandas: df.corr(method=...)
📊 FIGURE — Reading r at a glance
r ≈ +1: points hug a rising line. r ≈ 0: no linear pattern (though a CURVE can hide there — always plot!). r ≈ −1: tight falling line. Pearson measures LINEAR association only; Spearman ranks it, taming outliers and monotone curves.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Simple linear regression fits a straight line through paired data — the most-used predictive model in statistics. It tells you not just whether two variables are related (like correlation does) but exactly HOW: the slope, the predictions, and the residual errors. The DataCamp Data Scientist Associate exam tests fitting, interpreting coefficients, residual diagnostics, and the assumptions.

The model

SIMPLE LINEAR REGRESSION MODEL

y = β₀ + β₁ × x + ε

  β₀ = intercept (predicted y when x = 0)
  β₁ = slope (change in y per unit change in x)
  ε = error term (the unobserved noise)

We use sample data to estimate β̂₀ and β̂₁; predictions are ŷ = β̂₀ + β̂₁ × x.

Fitting — ordinary least squares (OLS)

LEAST SQUARES PRINCIPLE
Choose β̂₀, β̂₁ to MINIMIZE the sum of squared residuals:

SSR = Σ (yᵢ − ŷᵢ)² = Σ (yᵢ − β̂₀ − β̂₁ × xᵢ)²

Closed-form solutions:
  β̂₁ = Cov(x, y) / Var(x) = r × (σ_y / σ_x)
  β̂₀ = ȳ − β̂₁ × x̄ 
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

# Example: predict weight from height
height = np.array([60, 62, 65, 67, 68, 70, 72, 74, 76])
weight = np.array([110, 115, 130, 145, 150, 160, 175, 180, 195])

# Method 1: scipy's quick regression
result = stats.linregress(height, weight)
result.slope # ≈ 5.39 — each extra inch adds ~5.4 lb
result.intercept # ≈ -213.85
result.rvalue # correlation r
result.rvalue ** 2 # R² (variance explained)
result.pvalue # for testing slope ≠ 0
result.stderr # SE of the slope

# Predicted weight for someone 70 inches tall
predicted = result.intercept + result.slope * 70

# Method 2: NumPy polyfit (degree 1 = line)
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(height, weight, deg=1)

# Method 3: statsmodels — most informative
import statsmodels.api as sm
X = sm.add_constant(height) # add intercept column
model = sm.OLS(weight, X).fit()
print(model.summary()) # full regression output

Reading the model summary

Method: Least Squares F-statistic: 786.4
Date: [date] Prob (F-stat): 1.4e-08

Coefficients:

const -213.85 14.85 -14.4 0.000 -249.0 -178.7

# Key things to read:
# • coef (β̂): point estimates of intercept and slope
# • std err: SE of each estimate
# • t and P>|t|: test of "is this coefficient ≠ 0?"
# • CI 95%: confidence interval for the parameter
# • R-squared: variance explained
# • F-statistic, Prob (F-stat): test of "model better than nothing?"

Interpreting the slope and intercept

★ COEFFICIENT INTERPRETATION

Slope β̂₁ = 5.39: "For each additional inch of height, predicted weight increases by 5.4 lb." Always state UNITS.

Intercept β̂₀ = −213.85: "Predicted weight for someone 0 inches tall." Often nonsensical when x = 0 is outside the data range — use only as a baseline value.

Don't interpret coefficients beyond the range of your data. Extrapolation = high risk.

R-squared — fraction of variance explained

R² (COEFFICIENT OF DETERMINATION)

R² = 1 − (SS_res / SS_total)

  SS_res = Σ (yᵢ − ŷᵢ)² = sum of squared residuals
  SS_total = Σ (yᵢ − ȳ)² = total variance of y

R² = 0 means the model explains nothing (it'd predict the mean for everything).
R² = 1 means the model fits perfectly (all points on the line).

For simple regression, R² = r² (Pearson correlation squared).

Residuals and assumptions — LINE

LINEAR REGRESSION ASSUMPTIONS — LINE
Linearity — relationship between x and y is approximately linear
Independence — observations are independent
Normality — residuals are approximately normally distributed
Equal variance (homoscedasticity) — residual spread is constant across x

All four can be checked with residual plots. 
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.api as sm
import numpy as np

X = sm.add_constant(height)
model = sm.OLS(weight, X).fit()
predictions = model.predict(X)
residuals = weight - predictions

# Plot 1: Residuals vs predicted values
plt.scatter(predictions, residuals)
plt.axhline(0, color='r')
plt.xlabel('Predicted y')
plt.ylabel('Residuals')
# Should look like a random cloud around 0
# If there's a curve → nonlinearity (try a polynomial or transform x)
# If spread widens with predicted → heteroscedasticity (consider weighted regression)

# Plot 2: Q-Q plot of residuals (test normality)
from scipy import stats
stats.probplot(residuals, dist='norm', plot=plt)
# Points on the line → residuals are normal
# Curve → skewed; S-shape → heavy tails

# Plot 3: Residuals over time/order (if applicable)
# Detects autocorrelation in time-series data

Standard error of the regression and prediction

import numpy as np

# Residual standard error
n = len(height)
rss = np.sum(residuals ** 2)
rse = np.sqrt(rss / (n - 2)) # SD of residuals
# Quick interpretation: typical prediction error is ~RSE

# 95% confidence interval for the regression line at a given x
# (predicts the MEAN response, narrow)
# vs 95% prediction interval (predicts a NEW observation, wide)
# Always note which you mean

# statsmodels gives both
import statsmodels.api as sm
X = sm.add_constant(height)
model = sm.OLS(weight, X).fit()

# Confidence interval for the MEAN at each x
predictions = model.get_prediction(X)
ci_mean = predictions.conf_int(alpha=0.05) # narrow band

# Prediction interval for a NEW observation
ci_pred = predictions.summary_frame(alpha=0.05)
# Includes mean CI and obs_ci (the wider prediction interval)

Hypothesis testing on the slope

# H₀: β₁ = 0 (no linear relationship)
# H₁: β₁ ≠ 0
# Test statistic: t = β̂₁ / SE(β̂₁), df = n - 2

# scipy:
result = stats.linregress(height, weight)
result.pvalue # p-value for slope ≠ 0
result.stderr # SE(β̂₁)

# statsmodels gives a full summary
model.tvalues['x1'] # t for slope
model.pvalues['x1'] # p for slope
model.conf_int().loc['x1'] # 95% CI for slope

# For simple regression, the slope test is mathematically equivalent
# to testing the correlation: same p-value

Predicting and visualizing

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# Scatter plot with regression line and CI band
sns.regplot(x=height, y=weight)
# Built-in shading shows 95% CI for the regression line

# Manual prediction
new_height = np.array([60, 65, 70, 75, 80])
X_new = sm.add_constant(new_height)
predictions = model.predict(X_new)

# For prediction intervals (wider)
pred = model.get_prediction(X_new).summary_frame(alpha=0.05)
print(pred[['mean', 'mean_ci_lower', 'mean_ci_upper',
 'obs_ci_lower', 'obs_ci_upper']])
# mean_ci_* = 95% CI on the mean response (narrow, line CI)
# obs_ci_* = 95% prediction interval for a new observation (wide)

Common transformations for nonlinear relationships

# If residuals vs predicted shows curvature:
# Transform x, y, or both

# Right-skewed y → log(y)
y_log = np.log(y)

# Quadratic relationship → add x² as a feature (polynomial regression)
X_poly = np.column_stack([x, x**2])

# Multiplicative relationship → log both sides
# log(y) = β₀ + β₁ × log(x)
# Slope is now interpretable as: "% change in y per % change in x" (elasticity)

# Try these transformations BEFORE more complex models
# Often a log or polynomial transform fixes everything

Worked example — full regression workflow

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Years of experience vs salary

Scenario: Build a regression to predict salary from years of experience.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# Generate data
np.random.seed(42)
years = np.random.uniform(0, 25, 100)
salary = 40000 + 3500 * years + np.random.normal(0, 8000, 100)

# Step 1: EDA
df = pd.DataFrame({'years': years, 'salary': salary})
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x='years', y='salary')
# Looks linear

# Step 2: fit
X = sm.add_constant(df['years'])
model = sm.OLS(df['salary'], X).fit()
print(model.summary())

# Step 3: interpret
# Intercept (~40,000): predicted salary at 0 years
# Slope (~3,500): each additional year adds about $3,500
# R² ≈ 0.97 — explains 97% of variance
# p-value tiny → slope significantly different from 0

# Step 4: diagnostics
predictions = model.fittedvalues
residuals = model.resid
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))
axes[0].scatter(predictions, residuals)
axes[0].axhline(0)
axes[0].set_xlabel('Predicted'); axes[0].set_ylabel('Residuals')

from scipy import stats
stats.probplot(residuals, dist='norm', plot=axes[1])

# Step 5: predict a new value
new_years = pd.DataFrame({'const': 1, 'years': [10]})
pred = model.get_prediction(new_years).summary_frame(alpha=0.05)
print(pred[['mean', 'mean_ci_lower', 'mean_ci_upper',
 'obs_ci_lower', 'obs_ci_upper']])
# E.g., predicted salary at 10 years is $75,000 with 95% PI of $58k-$92k

# Reporting:
# "Each year of experience adds an estimated $3,500 to salary (95% CI: $3,300-$3,700, p < 0.001).
# R² = 0.97, indicating an excellent linear fit.
# Predictions are accurate to within ~$8,000 (residual SE)."

Common regression mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Interpreting the intercept beyond data range — extrapolation; sometimes the intercept has no real-world meaning
  2. Confusing CI on the line with prediction interval for new observations — the latter is much wider
  3. Not checking residual plots — masks nonlinearity, heteroscedasticity, outliers
  4. Ignoring outliers / high-leverage points — can dominate the fit
  5. Extrapolating outside the observed range of x — model fit doesn't guarantee accuracy outside the data
  6. Reporting R² without RMSE or SE — R² of 0.95 sounds great but predictions might still be off by $10k
  7. Confusing correlation with regression — correlation is symmetric (no x/y distinction); regression isn't
  8. Forgetting sm.add_constant(X) in statsmodels — without it, the model has no intercept
  9. Treating significant slope as evidence of causation — same caveat as correlation
  10. Heteroscedastic residuals — SE/CI/test results invalid; consider weighted regression or transform
★ ON THE EXAM

"Linear regression model?" → y = β₀ + β₁·x + ε.

"Slope interpretation?" → Change in y per 1-unit change in x.

"Intercept?" → Predicted y at x = 0 (may not be meaningful).

"OLS minimizes?" → Sum of squared residuals.

"R² formula?" → 1 − SS_res/SS_total; proportion of variance explained.

"R² for simple regression?" → Equal to r² (Pearson squared).

"Assumptions (LINE)?" → Linearity, Independence, Normality of residuals, Equal variance.

"Slope test?" → t = β̂₁ / SE(β̂₁); df = n − 2.

"CI for the line vs prediction interval?" → CI on mean is narrow; PI for new observation is wider.

"Detect nonlinearity?" → Plot residuals vs fitted; look for curvature.

"Detect heteroscedasticity?" → Residuals vs fitted; look for funnel shape.

"Extrapolation?" → Don't predict outside the range of training data.

"statsmodels OLS?" → sm.OLS(y, sm.add_constant(X)).fit().

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Simple linear regression fits y = β₀ + β₁·x by minimizing sum of squared residuals (OLS)
  • Slope = expected change in y per unit increase in x; intercept = expected y when x = 0
  • R² = proportion of variance in y explained by x (R² = r² in simple regression)
  • Test slope ≠ 0 with t-statistic = β̂₁ / SE(β̂₁), df = n − 2
  • Significance of slope test ≡ significance of correlation test (same p-value)
  • LINE assumptions: Linearity, Independence, Normality of residuals, Equal variance
  • Diagnose all four with residual plots — should be a random cloud around 0
  • Curvature in residuals → nonlinearity (transform or add polynomial term)
  • Funnel shape → heteroscedasticity (transform y or use weighted regression)
  • Confidence interval on regression LINE (mean response) is narrower than prediction interval for NEW observation
  • Don't extrapolate beyond range of training data
  • Common transformations: log(y) for right-skew, x² for curves, log-log for elasticities
  • Significant regression ≠ causal relationship — same caveats as correlation
  • scipy stats.linregress for quick fits; statsmodels OLS for full diagnostics
📊 FIGURE — Least squares: the line that minimizes squared residuals
Each residual (red) is the vertical gap between a point and the line: observed − predicted. The regression line is THE line making the sum of squared residuals as small as possible. R² then reports what fraction of the y-variation the line explains.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Multiple regression extends linear regression to multiple predictors — the workhorse of predictive modeling, A/B test analysis with covariates, and most real-world data science. Interpreting coefficients in the presence of other variables is the most common source of errors. The DataCamp Data Scientist Associate exam tests fitting, interpretation, multicollinearity, dummy variables, and model selection.

The model

MULTIPLE LINEAR REGRESSION

y = β₀ + β₁x₁ + β₂x₂ + ... + βₚxₚ + ε

  βⱼ = effect of xⱼ on y, HOLDING ALL OTHER PREDICTORS CONSTANT
  β₀ = predicted y when ALL predictors are 0

Still fit by minimizing sum of squared residuals — same OLS idea, now with multiple slopes.

Fitting a multiple regression

import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm
import numpy as np

# Predict house price from square feet, bedrooms, age
df = pd.DataFrame({
 'price': [...],
 'sqft': [...],
 'beds': [...],
 'age': [...]
})

# statsmodels OLS
X = df[['sqft', 'beds', 'age']]
X = sm.add_constant(X) # add intercept column
y = df['price']
model = sm.OLS(y, X).fit()
print(model.summary())

# scikit-learn (more flexible, less stats output)
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
sklearn_model = LinearRegression()
sklearn_model.fit(df[['sqft', 'beds', 'age']], df['price'])
sklearn_model.intercept_ # β₀
sklearn_model.coef_ # [β₁, β₂, β₃]

Interpreting coefficients — "holding others constant"

★ CRUCIAL INTERPRETATION RULE

In multiple regression, βⱼ is the effect of xⱼ HOLDING ALL OTHER PREDICTORS CONSTANT.

So if β_sqft = 120, the interpretation is: "Each additional square foot is associated with $120 more in price, holding bedrooms and age constant."

This is different from simple regression where β captures the marginal/raw effect (which often confuses correlation and causation).

Coefficients can FLIP SIGN when you add a predictor — that's a clue about confounding.

Example: how coefficients can change with predictors added

import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm

# Simple regression: sales ~ ad spend
m1 = sm.OLS(df['sales'], sm.add_constant(df['ad_spend'])).fit()
# Coefficient on ad_spend might be 5.0 — "each $1 of ads → $5 in sales"

# Add a confounder: economic conditions
m2 = sm.OLS(df['sales'],
 sm.add_constant(df[['ad_spend', 'gdp_growth']])).fit()
# Coefficient on ad_spend might drop to 2.0 — most of the apparent effect was
# really due to good economy boosting both sales and ad budgets

# This is why "controlling for X" matters in observational studies
# But controls only fix things you measure — unmeasured confounders still bias estimates

R² and adjusted R²

R² vs ADJUSTED R²

R² = 1 − SS_res / SS_total

Adjusted R² = 1 − (1 − R²) × (n − 1) / (n − p − 1)

R² always INCREASES as you add predictors (even useless ones).
Adjusted R² PENALIZES added predictors — only goes up if the new variable improves fit MORE than expected by chance.

Always report adjusted R² for multi-predictor models. 
model.rsquared # R²
model.rsquared_adj # adjusted R²

# Difference grows as you add predictors:
# n = 100, p = 1: very small gap
# n = 100, p = 50: large gap (adjusted R² much lower)

F-test for overall model significance

model.fvalue # F-statistic for "are ANY of the betas nonzero?"
model.f_pvalue # p-value for that F-test

# H₀ for the F-test: β₁ = β₂ = ... = βₚ = 0 (all coefficients are zero)
# H₁: at least one is nonzero

# If F-test is significant, at least one predictor matters
# Then check individual t-tests for which ones

Categorical predictors — dummy variables

import pandas as pd

# Categorical variable: city ∈ {NYC, LA, Chicago}
df['city'] = ['NYC', 'LA', 'Chicago', 'NYC', ...]

# Convert to dummy variables (one-hot encoding)
df_encoded = pd.get_dummies(df, columns=['city'], drop_first=True)
# Creates city_LA and city_NYC columns
# Chicago is the "reference category" (omitted)

# drop_first=True is critical — avoids the "dummy variable trap" (perfect multicollinearity)

# Coefficients now interpret as differences from the reference:
# β_city_NYC = price difference between NYC and Chicago
# β_city_LA = price difference between LA and Chicago

# statsmodels formula API does this automatically
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
model = smf.ols('price ~ sqft + beds + C(city)', data=df).fit()
# C() tells statsmodels city is categorical

Interaction terms

import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

# Does the effect of sqft DEPEND on whether the house has a pool?
model = smf.ols('price ~ sqft * has_pool', data=df).fit()
# Expands to: price ~ sqft + has_pool + sqft:has_pool
# The interaction term sqft:has_pool tests "does sqft's effect depend on pool?"

# Interpretation:
# β_sqft: effect of sqft when has_pool = 0
# β_sqft:has_pool: additional effect of sqft when has_pool = 1
# Total effect of sqft for a pool-house: β_sqft + β_sqft:has_pool

# Significant interaction means the effect is NOT constant across the moderator

Multicollinearity — when predictors are correlated

VIF (VARIANCE INFLATION FACTOR)

VIF_j = 1 / (1 − R²_j)

Where R²_j is the R² from regressing predictor j on all OTHER predictors.

Rules of thumb:
  VIF < 5: probably fine
  VIF 5–10: caution
  VIF > 10: serious multicollinearity 
from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import variance_inflation_factor
import pandas as pd

X = df[['sqft', 'beds', 'baths', 'rooms_total', 'age']]
vif = pd.DataFrame()
vif['feature'] = X.columns
vif['VIF'] = [variance_inflation_factor(X.values, i) for i in range(X.shape[1])]
print(vif)
# E.g., 'rooms_total' might have VIF = 12 because it's nearly redundant with beds + baths

# Solutions:
# • Drop one of the correlated predictors
# • Combine them into an index (PCA, factor analysis)
# • Use regularized regression (Ridge, Lasso) — handle multicollinearity better
⚠ MULTICOLLINEARITY EFFECTS

When predictors are highly correlated:

  • Coefficient SEs INFLATE → wide CIs, low t-statistics, p-values close to nothing
  • Coefficients become UNSTABLE — small changes in data flip signs
  • The model's predictions can still be fine; just don't trust individual coefficients

It's a problem when you care about interpretation; less critical for pure prediction.

Diagnostics — same as simple regression, plus more

import statsmodels.api as sm
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

# Same checks as simple regression:
# 1. Residuals vs fitted — random cloud?
# 2. Q-Q plot of residuals — normality?
# 3. Residuals vs each predictor — any specific predictor causing issues?
# 4. Cook's distance — identify high-leverage observations

# Cook's distance
influence = model.get_influence()
cooks_d = influence.cooks_distance[0]

# Plot
plt.scatter(range(len(cooks_d)), cooks_d)
plt.axhline(4 / len(df), color='r', linestyle='--') # rule-of-thumb threshold
plt.xlabel('Observation'); plt.ylabel("Cook's distance")

# Observations above the threshold are influential — they substantially change
# the regression line. Investigate; consider robust regression if many points are influential.

Feature selection — when to add or drop predictors

# Don't add every variable just because data is available — overfitting risk

# Three main strategies:
# 1. Theory-driven: include variables that should affect y based on domain knowledge
# 2. Statistical: use AIC/BIC to compare models
# AIC = 2k - 2ln(L); lower is better
# BIC = k×ln(n) - 2ln(L); penalizes complexity more than AIC
# 3. Regularization: use Lasso (L1) or Ridge (L2) to shrink coefficients toward zero

model.aic # AIC
model.bic # BIC

# Backward elimination (manual):
# Start with all predictors → drop the one with highest p-value → refit → repeat

# Forward selection:
# Start empty → add the predictor that most improves the model → repeat

# Stepwise: combine forward + backward at each step

# Modern preference: regularization (Ridge/Lasso) for high-dimensional problems

# Lasso for automatic variable selection
from sklearn.linear_model import LassoCV
lasso = LassoCV(cv=5).fit(X, y)
# Coefficients that get shrunk to exactly 0 are "dropped" by Lasso

Worked example — multi-predictor housing model

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Housing price regression

Scenario: Predict house price from sqft, beds, baths, age, and neighborhood.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import variance_inflation_factor

np.random.seed(42)
n = 500
df = pd.DataFrame({
 'sqft': np.random.normal(2000, 600, n).clip(800, 5000),
 'beds': np.random.choice([2, 3, 4, 5], size=n),
 'baths': np.random.choice([1, 2, 3], size=n),
 'age': np.random.uniform(0, 50, n),
 'neighborhood': np.random.choice(['downtown', 'suburb', 'rural'], size=n),
})
df['price'] = (
 100000
 + 200 * df['sqft']
 + 15000 * df['beds']
 - 1500 * df['age']
 + np.where(df['neighborhood'] == 'downtown', 50000,
 np.where(df['neighborhood'] == 'rural', -30000, 0))
 + np.random.normal(0, 30000, n)
)

# Fit
model = smf.ols('price ~ sqft + beds + baths + age + C(neighborhood)', data=df).fit()
print(model.summary())

# Check VIF on numeric predictors
X = df[['sqft', 'beds', 'baths', 'age']]
vif = pd.DataFrame({
 'feature': X.columns,
 'VIF': [variance_inflation_factor(X.values, i) for i in range(X.shape[1])]
})
print(vif)
# Likely shows beds and baths somewhat correlated (~1.5 VIF) — fine
# If any > 5, consider dropping

# Interpretation example (from summary):
# Intercept (~100,000): baseline price for the reference neighborhood with 0 sqft, 0 age, 0 beds
# (often not meaningful, just a starting point)
# sqft coef (~200): each extra sqft → $200 more, holding other things constant
# beds coef (~15,000): each extra bedroom → $15k more, holding sqft fixed
# (note: this is the effect of beds INDEPENDENT of sqft — counterintuitive but correct)
# age coef (~-1,500): older = cheaper by $1,500 per year
# C(neighborhood)[T.suburb] = ~0: not different from downtown baseline (in this example)
# C(neighborhood)[T.rural] = ~-30000: rural houses ~$30k less than downtown

# Reporting:
# "Predictors explain 90% of variance (adjusted R² = 0.90).
# Square footage adds about $200/sqft. Each bedroom contributes ~$15k beyond sqft.
# Older homes lose ~$1,500/year. Downtown homes sell for $30-50k more than rural."

Logistic regression — for binary outcomes

# When y is binary (success/fail, converted/not), use logistic instead of linear
# Models the LOG-ODDS as a linear function of predictors

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
import statsmodels.api as sm

# scikit-learn version
log_model = LogisticRegression()
log_model.fit(X, y_binary)
log_model.predict_proba(X_new) # probability predictions

# statsmodels version (full statistical output)
X_with_const = sm.add_constant(X)
sm_log = sm.Logit(y_binary, X_with_const).fit()
print(sm_log.summary())

# Coefficient interpretation: log-odds
# exp(β) → odds ratio per 1-unit increase in predictor

# Used heavily for classification, credit scoring, churn prediction, A/B tests
# with binary outcomes

Common multiple-regression mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Forgetting "holding others constant" when interpreting coefficients
  2. Dummy variable trap — including all k dummies instead of k − 1 → perfect multicollinearity
  3. Ignoring multicollinearity — check VIF; high VIF makes coefficients unstable
  4. Throwing in every variable available — overfitting; use adjusted R² or BIC to compare
  5. Confusing R² (always rises) with adjusted R² (only rises if new variable helps)
  6. Skipping diagnostics — residual plots and influential-point checks matter more in multi-predictor models
  7. Interpreting one coefficient without considering correlated predictors — they can flip sign together
  8. Using linear regression for binary outcomes — use logistic regression
  9. Forgetting to standardize features when comparing coefficient magnitudes across predictors with different scales
  10. Treating "controls" as making causal claims valid — only randomization fixes confounding completely
★ ON THE EXAM

"Multiple regression formula?" → y = β₀ + β₁x₁ + ... + βₚxₚ + ε.

"βⱼ interpretation?" → Effect of xⱼ on y, HOLDING ALL OTHER PREDICTORS CONSTANT.

"R² vs adjusted R²?" → R² always rises with more predictors; adjusted R² penalizes added predictors.

"Categorical predictor?" → Convert to k−1 dummy variables (drop_first=True).

"Dummy variable trap?" → Including ALL k dummies creates perfect collinearity.

"Multicollinearity diagnosis?" → VIF; concerning above 5, serious above 10.

"Multicollinearity solutions?" → Drop redundant predictor, combine, or regularize (Ridge/Lasso).

"F-test in multiple regression?" → H₀: all βⱼ = 0; tests if model is better than nothing.

"Interaction term?" → Tests if effect of one predictor depends on another.

"AIC vs BIC?" → Both penalize complexity; BIC penalizes more.

"Binary outcome?" → Logistic regression, not linear.

"Cook's distance?" → Measures observation's influence on the regression; check for outliers.

"statsmodels formula?" → smf.ols('y ~ x1 + x2 + C(cat) + x1:x2', data=df).fit().

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Multiple regression: y = β₀ + β₁x₁ + ... + βₚxₚ + ε; each β interpreted "holding others constant"
  • Same OLS estimation as simple regression, generalized to many predictors
  • R² always rises with more predictors; use adjusted R² for fair comparison
  • F-test of overall significance: H₀: all βⱼ = 0
  • Categorical predictors → k − 1 dummy variables (drop_first=True to avoid the trap)
  • Interaction terms test whether one predictor's effect depends on another
  • Multicollinearity: predictors strongly correlated with each other; check VIF (concerning > 5)
  • High VIF inflates SEs, makes coefficients unstable, but doesn't necessarily hurt predictions
  • Diagnostics: residuals vs fitted, Q-Q plot, Cook's distance for influential points
  • Feature selection: AIC/BIC, regularization (Lasso/Ridge), or theory-driven inclusion
  • For binary outcomes, use logistic regression — not linear
  • Coefficients can change sign when adding correlated predictors (confounding)
  • Controlling for variables doesn't equal causation; only randomization does
  • statsmodels OLS is the standard for inference; sklearn for production-ML pipelines
  • Standardize features before comparing coefficient sizes across different scales
📊 FIGURE — Least squares: the line that minimizes squared residuals
Each residual (red) is the vertical gap between a point and the line: observed − predicted. The regression line is THE line making the sum of squared residuals as small as possible. R² then reports what fraction of the y-variation the line explains.

Formulas & method

Center. Mean = (Σx)/n. Median = middle value of sorted data (average of two middles if n is even). Mode = most frequent value.

Spread. Population variance σ² = Σ(x−μ²)/n; sample variance s² = Σ(x−x̄)²/(n−1). Standard deviation is the square root of the variance.

Probability. For equally likely outcomes P(E) = (favorable)/(total). For a union, P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B). For independent events, P(A∩B) = P(A)·P(B).

Counting. Combinations C(n,k) = n!/(k!(n−k)!) count unordered selections. A probability of drawing a specific subset is (favorable combinations)/(total combinations).

Binomial. P(X=k) = C(n,k)·pᵏ·(1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ.

Expected value. E(X) = Σ x·P(x).

Mini-example

Data 3, 5, 8, 8, 11: mean = 35/5 = 7, sorted median = 8, mode = 8. Deviations from 7 are −4, −2, 1, 1, 4; squares 16, 4, 1, 1, 16 sum to 38, so σ² = 38/5 = 7.6.

"},"DC-STATS/solving/sv2":{"body":"

Formulas & method

z-score. z = (x − μ)/σ tells how many standard deviations x sits from the mean.

Empirical rule. For a normal distribution about 68% of values fall within 1σ of the mean, 95% within 2σ, and 99.7% within 3σ. Because the curve is symmetric, the area above μ+1σ is (100%−68%)/2 = 16%.

z-table. Φ(z) = P(Z < z). Then P(Z > z) = 1 − Φ(z).

Margin of error. For a mean, ME = z·(σ/√n); for 95% confidence z = 1.96.

Test statistics. Known σ: z = (x̄ − μ₀)/(σ/√n). Unknown σ (use s): t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n).

Two-tailed p-value. p = 2·P(Z > |z|).

Bayes' theorem. P(D | +) = [P(+|D)·P(D)] / [P(+|D)·P(D) + P(+|¬D)·P(¬D)].

Mini-example

If x̄ = 52, μ₀ = 50, σ = 8, n = 64, then σ/√n = 8/8 = 1 and z = (52−50)/1 = 2.0.

Formulas & method

These problems mix descriptive statistics and probability. Learn the formula, plug in the numbers, then simplify.

Center

  • Mean = Σx / n
  • Median = the middle value of the ordered data (average the two middle values if n is even)
  • Mode = the most frequently occurring value

Spread (watch the denominator!)

  • Population variance σ² = Σ(x − μ)² / N
  • Sample variance s² = Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1)
  • Standard deviation = √variance

A common mistake is dividing by N when the sample formula (n − 1) is required, or the reverse. Read the problem carefully.

Probability

  • Basic: P(A) = favorable outcomes / total outcomes
  • Combinations: C(n, r) = n! / (r!(n − r)!)
  • Binomial: P(X = k) = C(n, k) · p^k · (1 − p)^(n − k)
  • Expected value: E(X) = Σ x · P(x)

Worked mini-example

Data 2, 4, 6, 8 with μ = 5. Squared deviations: 9, 1, 1, 9, summing to 20. Population variance = 20 / 4 = 5, so σ = √5 ≈ 2.24. The sample variance would instead be 20 / 3 ≈ 6.67.

Formulas & method

These problems use the normal model and the basics of inference. Identify the quantity asked for, choose the matching formula, and substitute.

Standardizing

  • z-score: z = (x − μ) / σ
  • Empirical rule: about 68% within 1σ, 95% within 2σ, 99.7% within 3σ of the mean
  • z-table: gives P(Z less than z); by symmetry P(Z greater than z) = 1 − P(Z less than z)

Confidence & margin of error

  • Mean: ME = z* · σ / √n
  • Proportion: ME = z* · √(p̂(1 − p̂) / n)
  • For 95% use z* = 1.96; for 90% use z* = 1.645

Test statistics

  • z-test (σ known): z = (x̄ − μ₀) / (σ / √n)
  • t-test (σ unknown): t = (x̄ − μ₀) / (s / √n)

Decisions

Two-tailed p-value = 2 · P(Z greater than |z|). A frequent error is reporting the one-tailed value (half as large) and rejecting when you should not. Reject H₀ only when p ≤ α.

Bayes

P(A | B) = P(B | A) · P(A) / P(B), where P(B) sums over all ways B can occur.

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.
